MedX Technical Solution Design

The technical design of MedX, a platform for teleconsultations, lifelong patient records and prescription tracking. Every choice follows MedX's own priorities: health data is protected at rest and in transit, records cannot be silently rewritten, and authorised professionals reach critical information in seconds during an emergency.

0.1 MedX in one paragraph

MedX is a healthcare platform with three pillars: telehealth consultations (book, meet a doctor by video, chat and share documents), patient records management (a secure, lifelong medical record available to the patient and to the professionals who treat them) and prescription tracking (doctors issue e-prescriptions that pharmacies receive, prepare and dispense, while the patient follows every step). Because MedX handles health data — the most sensitive category of personal data — the architecture is driven first by data protection, record integrity and emergency availability, then by the care workflows, and last by business-support features.

0.2 Actors

Actor Description Main channels Typical actions
Patient Adult user; can also act as proxy (parent of a minor, caregiver with consent) Mobile app (iOS/Android), web app Book, attend consultations, read records, follow prescriptions, pay
Doctor / practitioner Verified health professional (license checked against the national registry) Web portal (desktop), mobile app Manage availability, run consultations, write notes, prescribe
Emergency clinician Practitioner holding the emergency_access entitlement (ER, on-call, EMS) Web portal, mobile app Break-glass access to a patient's critical information
Pharmacy staff Pharmacist, technician, pharmacy administrator Pharmacy portal, or their pharmacy management system (PMS) through the partner API Receive prescriptions, update status, answer patient inquiries
MedX operations Support agent, billing agent, platform administrator, privacy officer / DPO, auditor Back-office console (VPN + SSO + hardware MFA) Support without clinical data, audits, break-glass reviews
External systems Calendars, payment provider, SMS/e-mail/push providers, pharmacy systems, drug database, national health services, identity federation APIs, webhooks Integration

0.3 Scope

In scope — the eight business components of Appendix 1 plus the platform capabilities they need:

  1. User Management (identity, authentication, authorization, preferences)
  2. Teleconsultation Scheduling (booking, waitlists, urgent requests, external calendars)
  3. Consultation (virtual rooms, video/audio, chat, file transfer)
  4. Patient Records Management (medical history, notes, documents, emergency access)
  5. Prescription Management
  6. Pharmacy Interface
  7. Notification
  8. Billing & Payment

Platform capabilities: API & real-time gateways, policy engine, event bus, secure document store, audit trail, key management, observability, de-identified data platform.

Out of scope for v1 (kept compatible with the design): in-clinic practice management, medical imaging (PACS/DICOM viewers — only document uploads and links), insurance claim processing (third-party payer), AI-assisted diagnosis, connected medical devices. They are listed in the roadmap.

0.4 MedX priorities and how they drive the design

The brief is explicit: protecting data in transit and at rest is paramount and health professionals must access patient information promptly in emergencies. Each High-priority requirement is therefore turned into a non-negotiable architecture principle, not just a feature.

Priority Requirement Turned into…
High H1 Data privacy (encryption at rest & in transit) TLS 1.3 / mTLS everywhere, AES-256 at rest everywhere, per-patient envelope encryption of clinical data (principle P1)
High H2 Patient records management Dedicated FHIR-based Records service, versioned & audited (P3, P4)
High H3 Emergency access Break-glass capability on an isolated, Tier-0 read path with post-hoc review (P2)
High H4 Authentication & authorization Proven IdP (OIDC, MFA) + RBAC + ABAC policy engine, zero trust between services (P1)
High H5 Data integrity & secure file storage Append-only history, hash chaining, checksums, immutable backups, scanned & encrypted document store (P3)
Medium M1–M5 Scheduling, consultations, prescriptions, masking, calendars Core care workflows built on the High-priority foundation
Low L1–L6 Pharmacy, preferences, notification tracking, anonymization, billing, refunds Designed now, delivered last, bought rather than built when possible (PSP, messaging providers)

0.5 Architecture principles

ID Principle What it means in practice
P1 Privacy & security by design and by default Encrypt everything, least privilege, deny by default, data minimisation (no health data in SMS, e-mails, calendars, logs or events).
P2 Patient safety first The emergency access path must keep working when everything else is degraded: isolated deployment, minimal dependencies, highest availability tier.
P3 Integrity over convenience Clinical data is never overwritten or physically deleted during its retention period: every change is a new, attributed, tamper-evident version.
P4 Standards over custom HL7 FHIR R4 (+ International Patient Summary), OpenID Connect / OAuth 2.1, WebRTC, OpenAPI 3.1, CloudEvents. Easier interoperability, audits and hiring.
P5 Loose coupling, strong ownership One service = one bounded context = one private datastore. Services integrate through versioned APIs and domain events.
P6 Buy commodity, build differentiators Reuse an IdP, a payment provider, messaging providers, an open-source SFU. Build what makes MedX unique: records, emergency access, care workflows.
P7 Scale out and automate Stateless services, horizontal autoscaling, infrastructure as code, GitOps, no manual changes in production.
P8 Observable and auditable by default Every request traced, every access to health data audited in an immutable trail.

0.6 Assumptions

ID Assumption Impact on the design
A1 MedX launches in the EU (France first); the US is a possible later market. GDPR + French HDS certification (health-data hosting) are mandatory; the design is HIPAA-ready (BAAs, audit, encryption) for a later US cell.
A2 Hosting on a public cloud with HDS certification (reference implementation: AWS Paris region, DR in Frankfurt; Azure, Google Cloud or OVHcloud are equivalent options). Managed services are used only when they are inside the provider's certified scope. All health data stays in the EEA.
A3 Legal roles (controller / processor) between MedX and practitioners are defined by the DPO. The design supports both: per-practitioner access control, consent registry, full audit.
A4 Patients use a recent smartphone or browser supporting WebRTC; some have poor connectivity. Adaptive bitrate, audio-only fallback, TURN relays, mobile-first UX.
A5 Pharmacies use heterogeneous management systems, some without APIs. Web portal for everyone + adapter-based partner API for connected systems.
A6 Payments are processed by a PCI DSS Level 1 payment service provider (PSP). MedX never stores card data → minimal PCI scope (SAQ A).
A7 Doctors use Google Workspace, Microsoft 365 or CalDAV calendars. Connectors for the three families, free/busy only.
A8 Integration with national services (e-prescription, national health identifier, shared medical record) comes after v1. Records and prescriptions are modelled in FHIR to make these integrations adapters, not redesigns.
A9 Growth targets below are planning figures, to be re-validated each quarter. Capacity is designed with ×2 headroom and a clear scaling path beyond.

0.8 Service levels and criticality tiers

Services are grouped into criticality tiers. The tier sets the availability objective, the recovery objectives and the order in which capacity is protected when the platform is under stress.

Tier Scope Availability RPO RTO (region loss) RTO (zone loss)
Tier 0 — life-critical Emergency access, authentication/token validation, records read path 99.99 % 0 in-region (synchronous multi-AZ), ≤ 1 min cross-region ≤ 15 min automatic, < 1 min
Tier 1 — care delivery Records write, consultation, scheduling, prescription, chat 99.95 % 0 in-region, ≤ 1 min cross-region ≤ 1 h automatic, < 2 min
Tier 2 — support Pharmacy interface, notification, billing, analytics 99.9 % ≤ 5 min ≤ 4 h automatic, < 5 min
Capability Tier Latency objective (p95)
Emergency access — critical summary 0 < 300 ms API, < 1 s on screen
Login / token issuance 0 < 300 ms (excluding user MFA interaction)
Patient record read / write 1 < 300 ms / < 500 ms
Video consultation 1 join < 3 s; < 100 ms RTT to the nearest media node; mouth-to-ear < 400 ms
Chat message delivery 1 < 500 ms

0.9 Glossary

Term Meaning
PHI Protected Health Information — any health data linked to an identifiable person ("données de santé" under GDPR art. 9).
HDS Hébergeur de Données de Santé — French certification mandatory for hosting health data.
FHIR HL7 Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources — the standard data model and REST API for health data.
IPS International Patient Summary (HL7 FHIR IG) — minimal clinical summary designed for unplanned care; basis of the MedX emergency summary.
Break-glass Controlled override that grants immediate access in an emergency, with justification and mandatory review.
RBAC / ABAC Role-Based / Attribute-Based Access Control.
PDP / PEP Policy Decision Point (evaluates rules) / Policy Enforcement Point (enforces the decision in each service).
DEK / KEK Data Encryption Key / Key Encryption Key (envelope encryption).
HSM / KMS Hardware Security Module / Key Management Service.
SFU / TURN Selective Forwarding Unit (video router) / relay server used when a direct media path is impossible.
WORM Write Once, Read Many — storage that cannot be altered or deleted before its retention expires.
RPO / RTO Recovery Point Objective (max data loss) / Recovery Time Objective (max downtime).
SLO Service Level Objective.
INS / RPPS / FINESS French national patient health identifier / practitioner registry number / health establishment (pharmacy) registry number.
PSP Payment Service Provider (e.g., Stripe, Adyen).
Outbox pattern Events are written in the same database transaction as the business change, then published — no lost or phantom events.

1. High-Level Architecture

Deliverable 1. Visual representation of the overall structure of MedX and the logic behind it. Assumptions and targets come from 0. Context.

1.1 Architecture at a glance

Vector source: diagrams/medx-high-level-architecture.svg. Circled numbers ①–⑧ are the components of Appendix 1; H / M / L badges are MedX priorities (Appendix 2).

Seven ideas to remember

  1. Eight business microservices, one per component of Appendix 1, grouped into security zones. The clinical zone concentrates health data (PHI) and receives the strictest controls.
  2. One hardened front door. Only the edge (CDN/WAF, API gateway, real-time gateway, media plane) is reachable from the internet; every service and datastore lives in private subnets.
  3. Identity is centralised, enforcement is local. A proven identity provider issues tokens; a policy engine (OPA) runs next to each service so every request is authorised in about a millisecond without a network hop.
  4. Events first, synchronous calls only when a user is waiting. State changes are published as domain events on Kafka through a transactional outbox; this keeps services decoupled and failures contained.
  5. Each service owns its data (database-per-service). PostgreSQL is the default; specialised stores are used only where a clear need exists (Redis, Cassandra, object storage, OpenSearch).
  6. Security-critical capabilities are built once, as platform services: audit trail, secure document store, key management, observability & SIEM, de-identified data platform.
  7. Emergency access is a Tier-0 path: an isolated deployment that reads pre-computed summaries from replicas in two regions and depends on nothing that is not strictly necessary.

1.2 System context (C4 level 1)

MedX serves five groups of people and relies on seven families of external systems. Every external system sits outside the trust boundary: it only receives the data it needs (for example, calendars get free/busy slots and a generic "MedX teleconsultation" title — never a patient name or a specialty), through adapters owned by the consuming service.

1.3 Architectural style and rationale

Option Strengths Weaknesses for MedX Verdict
Monolith Simple to build and deploy One blast radius for PHI and payments; video, records and billing cannot scale independently; one bug can take down emergency access Rejected
Modular monolith Clear modules, simple operations Still one runtime and one database: no isolation of the Tier-0 path, compliance scopes (PHI, PCI) cannot be separated Good start-up option, rejected at MedX's target scale
Microservices by bounded context (8 business services + platform) Isolation of sensitive data and of failures, independent scaling (video ≠ records ≠ billing), independent release cadence, clear ownership Operational complexity, distributed data consistency Chosen — complexity mitigated below
Serverless functions everywhere No servers to operate, pay-per-use Cold starts on the emergency path, hard long-lived WebSocket/WebRTC sessions, vendor lock-in, harder HDS scoping Used only for small event handlers if useful

Why the chosen style fits the priorities

  • Data privacy (H1) and compliance: PHI is confined to the clinical zone; billing sits in a separate payment zone so its PCI scope stays minimal; the notification service never stores health data.
  • Emergency access (H3): the break-glass path is deployed separately (bulkhead) and cannot be starved by a spike in bookings or video traffic.
  • Scalability: the media plane scales on bandwidth, the records service on read throughput, the notification service on queue depth — each with its own autoscaling metric.

How the complexity is kept under control

  • The number of services is deliberately limited to the business components (no nano-services).
  • A golden-path service template gives every service the same skeleton: OpenAPI contract, authorization hook, outbox, health checks, OpenTelemetry, security headers, CI pipeline.
  • A service mesh provides mTLS, retries, timeouts and circuit breaking uniformly.
  • A platform team owns Kubernetes, the event bus, observability, and the security building blocks.

1.4 Layers and components

Layer Components Responsibility
Channels Patient mobile app (iOS/Android), patient web app, doctor web portal, pharmacy portal, back-office console User interfaces. No business logic, minimal local storage of health data (encrypted, wiped on logout).
Edge CDN + WAF + DDoS protection · API Gateway · Real-time Gateway (WebSocket) · Media plane (WebRTC SFU + TURN/STUN) Single entry point: TLS termination, token validation, rate limiting, request validation, routing, webhook ingress, real-time fan-out, media relay.
Identity & access ① User Management (+ Keycloak IdP) · Policy Decision Point (OPA) Who you are (authentication, MFA, federation) and what you may do (RBAC + ABAC, consent, care relationships, masking obligations).
Clinical zone ② Scheduling · ③ Consultation · ④ Patient Records + Emergency Access · ⑤ Prescription · ⑥ Pharmacy Interface Care workflows and health data.
Engagement zone ⑦ Notification Multi-channel messages without health details, preferences, delivery/read tracking.
Payment zone ⑧ Billing & Payment Fees, pre-authorisation and capture, invoices, refunds, ledger — card data stays at the PSP.
Event backbone Apache Kafka + schema registry + outbox relay (CDC) Asynchronous integration, audit feed, projections.
Platform services Audit trail · Secure document store · Keys & secrets (KMS/HSM, Vault) · Observability & SIEM · De-identified data platform Shared, security-critical capabilities.
Data layer PostgreSQL (one database per service) · Redis · Cassandra · Object storage · OpenSearch · Backup vault Persistence — see 3. Data model & storage.

Detailed responsibilities, APIs, events and flows of each component are in 2. Detailed component designs.

1.5 Security zones and trust boundaries

Zone Contains Data allowed Main controls
Edge (public) CDN/WAF, gateways, media nodes Encrypted traffic in transit only; no datastore WAF rules, DDoS protection, TLS 1.3, token validation, rate limits
Identity & access User Management, IdP, PDP Identity, credentials (hashed), roles, preferences MFA, credential hashing, admin JIT access, separate database
Clinical (PHI) Scheduling, Consultation, Records, Emergency Access, Prescription, Pharmacy Interface, Document Store Health data, per-patient encrypted Dedicated node pool, strict network policies, ABAC on every request, field-level encryption, full audit
Engagement Notification Contact details, preferences, message metadata — no PHI Templates reviewed for PHI, provider DPAs, opt-in/opt-out
Payment Billing & Payment Amounts, invoices, PSP tokens — no card numbers, no diagnosis Separate namespace & network policy, PSP hosted fields, webhook signatures
Platform Audit, KMS/Vault, observability, data platform Audit records (restricted), keys (never exported), logs scrubbed of PHI, de-identified datasets Separate security account for audit/logs, WORM storage, separation of duties
Non-production Dev, staging, demo Synthetic or anonymised data only Separate accounts, no network path to production

Flow rules across boundaries

  • Health data leaves the clinical zone only (a) towards an authorised user through the gateway, (b) towards a pharmacy through the Pharmacy Interface, minimised to what dispensing requires, or (c) towards the de-identified data platform after anonymisation.
  • Events on the bus carry identifiers and status, not clinical content ("claim-check" pattern: consumers fetch details from the owning service under their own authorisation).
  • Nothing in the clinical zone accepts inbound connections from the internet except through the gateways.

1.6 Communication patterns

Pattern Used for Protocol & format Rules
Synchronous request/response User-facing reads and commands; checks that need an immediate answer (e.g., allergy check while prescribing) HTTPS/REST, JSON, OpenAPI 3.1; FHIR R4 REST for clinical data; internal calls over mTLS Timeouts on every call, retries only for idempotent operations (with jitter), circuit breakers, at most two synchronous hops per user request, Idempotency-Key on every create
Asynchronous domain events Propagating state changes (booking, prescription, payment…), notifications, projections, audit Kafka topics, CloudEvents envelope, versioned schemas (schema registry, backward compatible) Published through the transactional outbox (no dual writes); at-least-once delivery + idempotent consumers; ordering by aggregate key (e.g., appointmentId)
Real-time push Chat, live statuses (prescription, queue position), in-app notifications WebSocket (WSS) via the Real-time Gateway, backed by pub/sub Authenticated at connection time, per-user channels, re-authorised on token refresh
Media Video and audio WebRTC: DTLS-SRTP (+ E2EE with SFrame when supported), ICE/STUN/TURN Media never transits through business services; rooms and tokens controlled by the Consultation service
External integration Calendars, PSP, messaging, pharmacy systems, drug database, national services REST/FHIR over TLS or mTLS, OAuth 2.0; inbound webhooks through the API gateway One adapter (anti-corruption layer) per external system, owned by the consuming service; signed webhooks; retries with backoff; dead-letter queues

1.7 Key end-to-end flows

1.7.1 The care journey: booking → consultation → prescription → pharmacy

1.7.2 How every request on health data is authorised

Two properties matter here: no access without an audit record (the audit event is written in the same database transaction as the read or write), and no network hop for the authorisation decision (OPA runs as a sidecar with policies distributed as signed bundles).

1.7.3 Emergency access (break-glass)

The detailed design (entitlement, grant model, critical summary content, review process) is in 2.4 Patient Records & Emergency Access.

1.8 Deployment view

  • Primary region in France (HDS-certified), spread over three availability zones. Every tier is redundant across zones: load balancers, Kubernetes node pools, database primary + synchronous standby + read replica, Redis replicas, three Kafka brokers, Cassandra and OpenSearch nodes.
  • Kubernetes node pools follow the security zones: gateway, identity, clinical (dedicated nodes) and support pools, plus a payment namespace isolated by network policy. Media nodes run in public subnets because WebRTC needs public UDP ports; they hold no data.
  • DR region (second EU region, EEA only) runs as a warm standby built from the same infrastructure-as-code: database replicas (lag < 1 s), Kafka mirror, replicated object storage, multi-region KMS keys. The Emergency Access API and the identity provider are active in both regions, so the Tier-0 path survives the loss of the primary region.
  • One cloud account per environment and purpose: production, DR, security & log archive (audit WORM, SIEM), shared services (CI/CD, signed images), non-production (synthetic data only).

The design is cloud-agnostic; the choices below are the reference implementation used for sizing and costing.

Concern Reference choice Why Alternatives

Compute Managed Kubernetes + Istio service mesh Standard autoscaling, uniform mTLS, traffic policies Linkerd; Nomad

Identity Keycloak (OIDC, MFA, WebAuthn/passkeys, identity brokering) Self-hostable inside the HDS scope, standards-based, no per-user fee Commercial IdPs if their hosting is HDS-compliant
Authorization Open Policy Agent (policies as code, sidecar) Low-latency local decisions, testable and versioned policies AWS Cedar, OpenFGA
Video LiveKit SFU (open-source) + TURN servers EU self-hosting, simulcast, E2EE support, horizontal scaling Jitsi, mediasoup; CPaaS (Vonage, Daily) if time-to-market dominates
Events Apache Kafka (managed) + schema registry + Debezium outbox relay Durable, replayable log, per-key ordering, high throughput RabbitMQ, NATS JetStream, Pulsar

Observability OpenTelemetry → Prometheus / Grafana / Loki / Tempo; SIEM Open standards, one correlation ID end-to-end Datadog, Elastic (hosting permitting)
Delivery CI pipelines, Argo CD (GitOps), Terraform, image signing (cosign), scanning (Trivy) Every change reviewed, reproducible and traceable Flux, Pulumi
Front-ends React + TypeScript (web), React Native (mobile) Shared skills and components across patient, doctor and pharmacy apps Native Swift/Kotlin

2.0 How to read this section

# Component Priority (Appendix 2) Zone Tier Document
① User Management (identity & access) HIGH (H4) · Low (L2 preferences) Identity & access 0 01-user-management.md
② Teleconsultation Scheduling Medium (M1, M5) Clinical 1 02-scheduling.md
③ Consultation (video, chat, files) Medium (M2) Clinical + media plane 1 03-consultation.md
④ Patient Records + Emergency Access HIGH (H2, H3, H5) · Medium (M4) Clinical 0 / 1 04-patient-records.md
⑤ Prescription Management Medium (M3) Clinical 1 05-prescription.md
⑥ Pharmacy Interface Low (L1) Clinical (minimised data) 2 06-pharmacy-interface.md
⑦ Notification Low (L2, L3) Engagement 2 07-notification.md
⑧ Billing & Payment Low (L5, L6) Payment 2 08-billing-payment.md

2.1 Common service blueprint

Every service is generated from the same golden-path template, so security and operability do not depend on each team's memory.

Concern Standard applied to every service
API contract OpenAPI 3.1 (FHIR CapabilityStatement for the Records service), URI versioning (/v1), additive changes only within a version, cursor pagination, errors as application/problem+json (RFC 9457), Idempotency-Key required on every POST that creates something.
Authentication JWT validated again in the service (defence in depth, even behind the gateway); service-to-service identity through mesh mTLS (SPIFFE IDs).
Authorization A Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) in the service calls the local OPA sidecar with subject · action · resource · purpose; deny by default; obligations (masking) applied before the response leaves.
Data Private database/schema and credentials (issued by Vault, 1 h TTL); reviewed migrations (Flyway); UUIDv7 identifiers (time-ordered, never sequential integers exposed to clients); outbox table for events.
Events CloudEvents envelope, schema in the registry, published via the outbox relay; consumers idempotent (processed-event table), dead-letter topic after 5 attempts.
Resilience ≥ 3 replicas spread over 3 AZs (Tier 0/1), readiness/liveness probes, graceful shutdown, pod disruption budgets, timeouts + retries with jitter + circuit breakers (mesh), bulkheads for critical paths.
Observability OpenTelemetry traces (W3C traceparent also propagated in Kafka headers), RED metrics, structured JSON logs without PHI (allow-listed fields, tokenised identifiers), SLO dashboard and alerts.
Delivery CI: unit, contract (consumer-driven) and integration tests, SAST, dependency and container scanning, signed images; CD: GitOps, canary release through the mesh with automatic rollback.

2.2 Synchronous dependencies

Synchronous calls are limited to cases where a user is waiting for an answer. The graph is acyclic and never deeper than two hops; everything else goes through events.

Caller → callee Why synchronous Failure handling
Scheduling → Billing The patient is waiting for the booking confirmation that depends on the payment authorisation Timeout 5 s, slot hold kept 10 min so the patient can retry; no retry on non-idempotent calls without the idempotency key
Consultation → Scheduling Join tokens are issued only to the appointment's participants within its time window Local replica of today's appointments (built from events) used if Scheduling is unavailable
Prescription → Records Allergy and interaction checks need the current allergy and medication lists On failure the doctor sees "safety check unavailable" and must explicitly acknowledge before signing
Pharmacy Interface → Prescription Pharmacies fetch the full prescription only when they open it (events carry identifiers only) Retries with backoff; the pharmacy portal shows the item as "loading"
Services → Document Store Upload/download of files Uploads resumable; downloads retried

2.3 Event catalogue

Topic naming: <domain>.<aggregate>.v<major>. Partition key = aggregate identifier (keeps per-aggregate ordering). Events carry identifiers, statuses and timestamps — never clinical content; consumers fetch details from the owning service under their own authorisation (claim-check).

Topic Events Producer Main consumers
identity.user.v1 UserRegistered, ProfileUpdated, PractitionerVerified, PractitionerSuspended, UserDeactivated, RoleAssigned, DelegationGranted/Revoked ① User Management ② (enable/disable agendas), ④ (create patient record & keys, revoke grants), ⑦, ⑧
identity.preferences.v1 PreferencesUpdated ① ⑦
scheduling.appointment.v1 AppointmentBooked, AppointmentRescheduled, AppointmentCancelled, AppointmentNoShow, AppointmentReminderDue, WaitlistSlotOffered, UrgentRequestCreated/Assigned ② ③ (plan rooms), ④ (care grants), ⑦, ⑧ (void/refund)
consultation.session.v1 ConsultationOpened, ConsultationStarted, ConsultationCompleted, ConsultationFailed, ChatTranscriptReady ③ ② (complete/no-show), ④ (encounter, transcript archive), ⑧ (capture or refund), ⑦
records.record.v1 RecordUpdated, DocumentAdded, ResultReleased, ConsentChanged ④ ④ projections (critical summary, timeline), ⑦ ("new document available")
records.emergency.v1 BreakGlassGranted, BreakGlassReviewDue, BreakGlassReviewed ④ Audit/SIEM (real-time alert), ⑦ (privacy office, patient notice)
