2.1 ① User Management Service — Identity & Access

Priority Zone Criticality Owns
HIGH — H4 authentication & authorization · Low — L2 user preferences Identity & access Tier 0 (login, token validation) Identities, profiles, roles, organisations, delegations, preferences

Mission — know who every user is, prove it strongly, and give every other service a trustworthy basis to decide what that user may do.

Responsibilities

Appendix 1 feature How MedX delivers it
Handle user registrations and profile updates Patients self-register (e-mail + phone verification). Access to their medical record requires a verified identity (FranceConnect or ID-document check). Doctors go through professional onboarding: licence number checked against the national registry (RPPS / Annuaire Santé), identity document, manual approval. Pharmacies register as organisations (FINESS number checked); the pharmacy administrator invites staff.
Authenticate users Keycloak identity provider: OpenID Connect Authorization Code + PKCE, mandatory MFA for all professionals (passkeys/WebAuthn, TOTP, or the professional smart card through Pro Santé Connect), risk-based MFA for patients, step-up for sensitive actions.
Authorize access based on user roles Coarse RBAC roles carried in tokens + fine-grained ABAC decisions by the policy engine (OPA) beside each service: care relationship, consent, purpose of use, data sensitivity, organisation.
Store and manage user preferences Preferences API (language, time zone, accessibility, notification channels per category, quiet hours, frequency caps). Changes are published as PreferencesUpdated so the Notification service applies them without calling back.

Internal design

  • Three realms isolate populations with different risks: patient policies favour usability (passkeys, biometrics on mobile), professional policies are strict (MFA always, 15-minute idle timeout, 12-hour absolute session), workforce identities come from the corporate IdP with hardware security keys.
  • Policies are code: Rego files in Git, unit-tested in CI (opa test), packaged as signed bundles pulled by the OPA sidecars. A policy change is reviewed like any code change and is fully traceable.
  • The service keeps attributes (roles, organisation memberships, entitlements such as emergency_access) and exposes them in tokens; facts that change per request (care grants, consents) are looked up by the calling service and passed to OPA as input.

Roles and permissions (RBAC layer)

Capability Patient Proxy Doctor Doctor + emergency_access Pharmacist / technician Support agent Privacy officer Platform admin
Manage own profile & preferences ✅ ✅ (delegated) ✅ ✅ ✅ — — —
Book / cancel consultations own dependant's — — — assist, no PHI — —
Manage availability & agenda — — own own — — — —
Read medical record own (with release rules) scoped with care grant + break-glass ❌ ❌ audit metadata only ❌
Write clinical notes upload own documents — with care grant emergency note ❌ ❌ ❌ ❌
Create / modify / revoke prescriptions — — own patients — ❌ ❌ ❌ ❌
View prescriptions own dependant's issued by self via break-glass assigned to their pharmacy only (minimised) ❌ ❌ ❌
Update fulfilment status — — — — ✅ ❌ ❌ ❌
Issue refunds request request — — — ≤ threshold (4-eyes above) — ❌
View audit trail own access history — — — — ❌ ✅ ❌
Operate infrastructure — — — — — — — JIT, time-boxed, no PHI

ABAC layer (illustrative policy)

RBAC answers "can a doctor read records?"; ABAC answers "can this doctor read this patient's record now, for this purpose?".

package medx.records

import rego.v1

default allow := false

# Treating doctor: verified, MFA-authenticated, holding an unexpired care grant for this patient
allow if {
    input.subject.role == "doctor"
    input.subject.verified
    input.subject.aal >= 2
    input.facts.care_grant.expires_at > input.now
    not sensitive_without_consent
}

# Break-glass: read-only, time-boxed, and never if the patient has lawfully opted out
allow if {
    "emergency_access" in input.subject.entitlements
    input.purpose_of_use == "ETREAT"
    input.action == "read"
    input.facts.emergency_grant.expires_at > input.now
    not input.facts.patient_opted_out_of_break_glass
}

sensitive_without_consent if {
    input.resource.security_label == "restricted"
    not input.facts.explicit_consent
}

# Obligations returned with the decision and applied by the service before responding
obligations contains {"mask": "psychotherapy-notes"} if input.purpose_of_use == "ETREAT"

Authentication flows

Audience Flow Factors Session & tokens
Patient mobile app OIDC Authorization Code + PKCE through the system browser Password or passkey; risk-based second factor (new device, record download); biometric unlock of the stored refresh token Access token 10 min, DPoP-bound (RFC 9449); refresh token rotated on every use, 30-day sliding window, device-bound
Patient web app Same, confidential client via a thin backend-for-frontend holding tokens server-side Same HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookies; no tokens in browser storage
Doctor / pharmacy portals OIDC Authorization Code + PKCE Mandatory MFA: passkey/WebAuthn, TOTP or professional smart card (e-CPS via Pro Santé Connect); SMS OTP not allowed (SIM-swap risk) Access token 5 min, idle timeout 15 min, absolute 12 h; step-up (max_age/acr) before signing a prescription or breaking the glass
Pharmacy systems (PMS) OAuth 2.0 client credentials mTLS client certificate, certificate-bound tokens (RFC 8705) Token 5 min, per-pharmacy scopes and rate limits
MedX workforce SSO with corporate IdP FIDO2 hardware key Privileged roles only through just-in-time elevation (approval, time-boxed, session recorded)

Token content — access tokens are JWTs signed with ES256 (keys rotated, published on the JWKS endpoint) and contain an opaque subject UUID, realm, roles, organisation, entitlements, authentication assurance (acr/amr) and audience. They never contain personal data (no name, no e-mail, no birth date).

Revocation — logout, password reset and account suspension revoke the refresh-token family immediately; the short access-token lifetime bounds the remaining exposure, and a denylist in Redis (checked by the gateway) cuts suspended accounts within seconds.

Account protection — passwords hashed with Argon2id (PBKDF2-SHA512 in FIPS mode), minimum 12 characters, breached-password check, no forced periodic rotation (NIST SP 800-63B); progressive rate limiting and lockout; bot detection on registration and login; alerts for logins from new devices; account recovery that never downgrades assurance (a professional who loses a factor goes through identity re-verification).

Key flows

Professional onboarding

Proxy access (delegation) — a parent is linked to a minor after document verification (the link expires at majority; care the minor asked to keep confidential is hidden from the parent by policy); an adult patient can delegate scoped rights (book, view prescriptions, view records) to a caregiver and revoke them at any time.

API (selection)

Method Endpoint Purpose
POST /v1/users Patient registration
POST /v1/practitioner-registrations Start professional onboarding
GET / PATCH /v1/users/me Read / update own profile
GET / PUT /v1/users/me/preferences Read / replace preferences (versioned, If-Match)
POST / DELETE /v1/users/me/delegations Grant / revoke proxy access
POST /v1/organizations/{orgId}/members Pharmacy administrator invites staff
POST /v1/admin/practitioner-registrations/{id}/decision Approve / reject (back-office, 4-eyes)
POST /v1/users/me/privacy-requests GDPR access/portability request, account closure
— /realms/{realm}/protocol/openid-connect/* Standard OIDC endpoints (authorize, token, JWKS, logout)

Data owned

PostgreSQL (usermgmt database) + Keycloak's own PostgreSQL database — details in §3.4. Contact data (phone, address, national identifier) is encrypted at field level; e-mail is stored encrypted with a blind index (keyed HMAC) so it can still be looked up for login without being readable.

Scalability & resilience

  • Token validation is local everywhere (gateway and services cache the JWKS), so the IdP only handles logins and refreshes: ~3 M per day at Year 3, about 35/s on average and 300/s at peak — modest, but password hashing is CPU-intensive, so login endpoints are rate-limited and Keycloak nodes sized on hashing cost.
  • Keycloak runs as a 3+ node cluster across AZs with a distributed session cache, active in both regions (Tier 0): clinicians can still sign in during a regional failover.
  • The User Management service itself is stateless and scales horizontally; profile reads are cached for 60 s.

Design decisions & trade-offs

Decision Alternative Why this choice
Reuse a proven IdP (Keycloak) Build authentication in-house Authentication is where custom code fails most dangerously; Keycloak brings OIDC, MFA, WebAuthn, brokering and audits. Cost: running and patching a stateful cluster.
Short-lived JWTs validated locally Opaque tokens + introspection on every call Removes the IdP from the hot path (latency, resilience of the emergency path). Cost: revocation is not instant → 5–10 min lifetimes + denylist for high-risk events.
RBAC + ABAC with OPA RBAC only RBAC alone cannot express care relationships, consent or break-glass. OPA keeps policies testable and versioned.
Separate realms per population One realm Different assurance levels and session rules; a misconfiguration on the patient side cannot weaken professional accounts.

2.2 ② Teleconsultation Scheduling Service

Priority Zone Criticality Owns
Medium — M1 scheduling · M5 external calendars Clinical (an appointment with a specialist is health data) Tier 1 Availability rules, appointments, waitlists, urgent requests, calendar connections

Mission — let patients find and book the right consultation in a few taps, never double-book a doctor, keep doctors informed in real time, and give urgent cases a faster lane.

Responsibilities

Appendix 1 feature How MedX delivers it
Book, reschedule, cancel consultations Slot search → short hold → confirmation with payment pre-authorisation (saga with Billing). Rescheduling moves the same appointment to a new held slot; cancellation applies the cancellation policy (free until 24 h before).
Notify doctors of new bookings or changes AppointmentBooked/Rescheduled/Cancelled events → Notification (push/e-mail per preferences) and live update of the doctor's agenda through the Real-time Gateway.
Integrate with doctors' calendars Connectors for Google Calendar, Microsoft 365 (Graph) and CalDAV: external busy times block MedX slots; MedX appointments are written back without any patient data.
Waitlists and priority scheduling for urgent cases Waitlist per doctor or specialty with automatic offers when a slot is released; triage questionnaire → urgency level; on-demand urgent queue served by on-call doctors; reserved urgent capacity.

Internal design

Module Role
Availability engine Computes free slots = recurring rules (RRULE, per consultation type) − exceptions (leave) − external busy blocks − booked/held slots − reserved urgent capacity. Pre-computes the next 60 days per doctor in Redis; recomputes incrementally on every relevant event.
Booking manager Holds, confirmations, rescheduling, cancellations; orchestrates the payment saga; owns the appointment state machine.
Waitlist & urgent queue Priority queues, slot offers with exclusive time-boxed holds, matching of urgent requests to on-call doctors.
Calendar sync OAuth connections, push-notification webhooks, incremental delta sync, outbound event writing, subscription renewal, nightly reconciliation.
Durable timers Database-backed scheduler (survives restarts) for hold expiry, reminders (T-24 h, T-1 h, T-10 min), waitlist offer expiry.
Directory projection Denormalised doctor profiles (specialty, languages, fees, next available slot) in OpenSearch for fast search.

Appointment lifecycle

Booking saga and double-booking prevention

Two independent safeguards prevent double booking:

  1. Fast path — an atomic Redis hold (SET … NX PX 600000) rejects concurrent attempts on the same slot in under a millisecond.
  2. Source of truth — a PostgreSQL exclusion constraint makes overlapping active appointments for a doctor physically impossible, even if Redis is unavailable or a bug bypasses the hold:
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS btree_gist;

ALTER TABLE appointment
  ADD CONSTRAINT appointment_no_overlap
  EXCLUDE USING gist (
    practitioner_id WITH =,
    tstzrange(starts_at, ends_at, '[)') WITH &&
  )
  WHERE (status IN ('HELD', 'PENDING_PAYMENT', 'BOOKED', 'IN_PROGRESS'));

Waitlist and urgent cases

  • Waitlist — a patient can wait for an earlier slot with a doctor or any doctor of a specialty. When a slot is released, the matcher offers it to the best candidate, ordered by urgency level then waiting time, with an exclusive 15-minute hold; if declined or expired, the next candidate gets it.
  • Triage — a short, medically validated questionnaire (rule-based, conservative) classifies the request: EMERGENCY (red flags → booking stopped, the app displays the emergency number 15/112), URGENT (same day), SOON (≤ 48 h), ROUTINE. Telehealth must never delay emergency care.
  • Urgent on-demand queue — URGENT requests enter a queue served by on-call doctors (matched on specialty, language, licence). A doctor has 2 minutes to accept before the request moves on; a supervisor dashboard tracks the waiting-time objective (< 30 min) and escalates.
  • Reserved capacity — doctors may reserve a share of their slots for urgent cases; unused reserved slots are released to everyone 2 hours in advance.

External calendar integration

Aspect Design
Providers Google Calendar API, Microsoft Graph (Outlook / Microsoft 365), CalDAV (Apple iCloud and others)
Consent & scopes Doctor connects through OAuth 2.0 with minimum scopes: read free/busy, write only MedX events (a dedicated "MedX" calendar where the provider supports it). CalDAV uses an app-specific password stored in Vault.
Inbound (busy times) Provider push notifications (Google watch channels, Graph change subscriptions) → webhook through the gateway → incremental fetch (sync token / delta link) → external_busy_block updated → availability recomputed within seconds. Fallback polling every 10 min; nightly full reconciliation; automatic renewal of expiring subscriptions.
Outbound (MedX bookings) Each booking creates an event titled "MedX teleconsultation" with a link to the portal — no patient name, no reason, no specialty. Reschedules and cancellations update or delete it (mapping appointment_id ↔ external_event_id, idempotent).
Data minimisation Only start/end of busy periods are stored — never titles, attendees or descriptions of the doctor's private events.
Conflicts MedX appointments are the source of truth. If the doctor adds an overlapping private event, MedX alerts the doctor; it never cancels a patient automatically.
Failures Per-provider rate-limit handling with exponential backoff and circuit breaker; if a provider is down, the last known busy blocks are used and the doctor sees a "calendar sync delayed" banner.
Secrets OAuth refresh tokens encrypted with Vault Transit, revoked when the doctor disconnects.

API (selection)

Method Endpoint Purpose
GET /v1/practitioners?specialty=&language=&date= Directory search (OpenSearch)
GET /v1/practitioners/{id}/slots?from=&to=&type= Free slots (Redis cache)
POST /v1/appointment-holds Hold a slot for 10 min
POST /v1/appointments Confirm booking (Idempotency-Key, holdId, payment method)
POST /v1/appointments/{id}/reschedule Move to another held slot
POST /v1/appointments/{id}/cancel Cancel with reason (policy → refund/void)
POST /v1/waitlist-entries Join a waitlist
POST /v1/urgent-requests Triage answers → urgent queue or emergency advice
PUT /v1/practitioners/me/availability-rules Doctor's recurring availability
POST /v1/practitioners/me/calendar-connections Start OAuth connection to an external calendar
POST /v1/webhooks/calendars/{provider} Provider push notifications (validated channel tokens)

Events

  • Publishes scheduling.appointment.v1: AppointmentBooked, AppointmentRescheduled, AppointmentCancelled, AppointmentNoShow, AppointmentReminderDue, WaitlistSlotOffered, UrgentRequestCreated, UrgentRequestAssigned.
  • Consumes billing.payment.v1 (PaymentAuthorized/Failed), consultation.session.v1 (Started/Completed → status), identity.user.v1 (PractitionerVerified enables the agenda; PractitionerSuspended freezes it and triggers patient rebooking).

Data owned

PostgreSQL: availability_rule, availability_exception, appointment (+ append-only appointment_history), waitlist_entry, urgent_request, calendar_connection, external_busy_block, timer, outbox. Redis: holds, per-doctor-day availability, waitlist queues. OpenSearch: doctor directory (public profile data only). Details in §3.4.

Security & privacy

  • Patients see only their own appointments; doctors only their own agenda; support agents see masked data.
  • Appointment reason and triage answers are health data: encrypted at field level, visible only to the patient and the booked doctor.
  • Directory search is public (profiles only) and protected by rate limiting and bot detection against scraping.

Scalability & resilience

  • Reads dominate (search and availability): served from OpenSearch and the Redis availability cache, so the database is not hit by browsing; cache entries are recomputed on events, not on reads.
  • Writes are modest (200 k bookings/day at Year 3 ≈ 2–3/s, peaks ≈ 30/s) and contention is local to one doctor.
  • Peaks (Monday 8–10 am, epidemics) are absorbed by autoscaling on request rate; if the payment provider is slow, holds keep the slot for the patient.

Design decisions & trade-offs

Decision Alternative Why this choice
Pre-computed availability Compute on every request Fast, predictable search under peak load. Cost: invalidation logic, bounded staleness (seconds).
Redis hold and DB exclusion constraint Only one of them Redis gives speed; the constraint gives a guarantee. Belt and braces for a problem users notice immediately.
Payment pre-authorisation at booking, capture after the consultation Pay at the end Reduces no-shows and failed payments; the patient pays only for a consultation that happened. Cost: authorisations expire after ~7 days → for distant appointments the card is saved (SCA) and authorised 24 h before.
Free/busy only, no PHI in external calendars Full two-way sync External calendars are outside MedX's trust boundary and HDS scope.

2.3 ③ Consultation Service — Video, Audio, Chat & Files

Priority Zone Criticality Owns
Medium — M2 consultation services Control plane in the clinical zone · media plane at the edge Tier 1 Virtual rooms, participants, session events, chat history (hot), call-quality telemetry

Mission — give patient and doctor a reliable, private virtual room: good video on a bad network, a chat that never loses a message, and a safe way to exchange medical documents.

Responsibilities

Appendix 1 feature How MedX delivers it
Create virtual rooms One room per appointment, planned when the appointment is booked and opened 15 min before; waiting room until the doctor admits the patient; unguessable 128-bit room identifiers.
Handle video and audio streaming WebRTC through a self-hosted SFU (LiveKit) with TURN/STUN relays; simulcast and adaptive bitrate; automatic audio-only fallback; reconnection with ICE restart.
Enable text chat during consultations Chat over the Real-time Gateway (WSS), persisted and ordered per room, with delivery/read receipts; transcript archived into the patient record at the end.
Allow file transfers for medical documents Uploads through the Secure Document Store (quarantine, antivirus, type checks, encryption); files shared in the chat; doctor can file them into the record.

Control plane vs media plane

  • The control plane (Consultation service) decides who may enter which room when; it never touches media.
  • The media plane (SFU + TURN) only forwards encrypted packets; it stores nothing and holds no health data at rest. Media nodes live in public subnets because WebRTC needs public UDP ports.

Room lifecycle

Joining a consultation

Tokens are short-lived, room-scoped and participant-scoped; the participant identity inside the SFU is a pseudonymous ID, never the patient's name. Additional participants (interpreter, caregiver) can be invited only with the patient's consent and receive their own scoped token.

Media quality on real-world networks

Technique Effect
Simulcast (3 layers) + dynacast Each receiver gets the layer its bandwidth supports; unused layers are paused to save uplink.
Opus audio with in-band FEC and DTX Speech stays intelligible up to ~20 % packet loss; audio is prioritised over video.
Congestion control (transport-wide CC) Bitrate adapts continuously; below ~150 kbit/s the call switches to audio-only automatically.
TURN over TLS on port 443 Works on restrictive hospital and corporate networks.
ICE restart + reconnect Moving from Wi-Fi to 4G does not end the consultation.
Pre-call test Camera, microphone and bandwidth checked before the patient enters the waiting room.
Quality telemetry WebRTC statistics (RTT, jitter, loss, freezes) sampled every 10 s — no media, no PHI — feed dashboards and alerts per region and per TURN node.

Privacy of the media

  • Hop-by-hop encryption is mandatory: WebRTC always uses DTLS-SRTP.
  • End-to-end encryption (E2EE) with insertable streams (SFrame) is on by default for 1-to-1 consultations when both devices support it: keys are negotiated between participants' devices and never stored by MedX, so neither MedX nor the SFU operator can decrypt audio or video.
  • No recording of consultations (privacy by design). If recording is ever introduced (e.g., for training), it would require explicit consent, disable E2EE for that session and be stored as a document of the record.

Chat

  • Exactly-once effect: at-least-once delivery + deduplication on clientMsgId; ordering by server time-UUID.
  • Retention: the hot store keeps messages 30 days (TTL) for convenience; when the consultation ends, the full transcript is archived into the patient record (ChatTranscriptReady → Records creates a document), which is the legal, long-term copy.
  • Typing indicators and presence are ephemeral (never stored).

File sharing

  1. The app asks the Document Store for an upload slot → pre-signed URL to a quarantine bucket (5 min validity, size ≤ 50 MB, allowed types: PDF, JPEG, PNG, HEIC).
  2. The file is scanned (antivirus, real type from magic bytes, PDF active content removed, image metadata such as GPS location stripped), then encrypted and moved to the documents bucket with its SHA-256 checksum.
  3. A "file shared" message referencing the document ID appears in the chat; downloads go through the Document Store with the same authorisation as the consultation and are audited.
  4. Files sent by the patient are attached automatically to the encounter as patient-provided documents; the doctor decides which files to file permanently into the record.

API (selection)

Method Endpoint Purpose
POST /v1/consultations/{id}/join Room token + SFU URL + ephemeral TURN credentials
POST /v1/consultations/{id}/admit Doctor admits the patient from the waiting room
POST /v1/consultations/{id}/participants Invite interpreter/caregiver (patient consent required)
POST /v1/consultations/{id}/end Doctor ends the consultation
GET /v1/consultations/{id}/messages?cursor= Chat history (paginated)
POST /v1/consultations/{id}/files Request an upload slot (delegated to the Document Store)
POST /v1/telemetry/webrtc Call-quality statistics
WSS /v1/realtime → channel consultation:{id} Chat, receipts, presence

Events

  • Publishes consultation.session.v1: ConsultationOpened, ConsultationStarted, ConsultationCompleted (duration, participants), ConsultationFailed (nobody could connect → automatic refund), ChatTranscriptReady.
  • Consumes scheduling.appointment.v1 (plan, move or cancel rooms).

Data owned

PostgreSQL (consultation, participant, session_event, quality_summary), Cassandra (chat_message, 30-day TTL, encrypted content), Redis (room → SFU node routing, presence). Files belong to the Document Store.

Scalability & resilience

  • Sizing (Year 3): 10 k concurrent sessions → 20 k participants; ~1.2 Mbit/s average per received stream → ~24 Gbit/s of SFU egress. At ~200 participants per 8-vCPU node (to be confirmed by load tests), about 100 media nodes at peak, autoscaled up to 200 for the ×2 headroom, spread over three AZs.
  • Placement: each 1-to-1 room lives on one node in the region closest to its participants; nodes are drained, never killed on scale-in (no new rooms, existing calls finish).
  • TURN capacity sized for ~20 % of sessions relayed (restrictive networks).
  • Failure of a media node: clients reconnect automatically to another node within seconds (ICE restart); the room state is re-created from the control plane.
  • Degraded mode: if video is impossible, audio-only; if media fails entirely, chat keeps working and the doctor can call the patient by phone (the event is logged).

Design decisions & trade-offs

Decision Alternative Why this choice
Self-hosted open-source SFU (LiveKit) Video CPaaS (Vonage, Daily…) Media stays on HDS-certified EU infrastructure; lower cost at scale; E2EE support. Cost: operating media servers (UDP, autoscaling, TURN). A CPaaS remains a fallback option for time-to-market.
SFU Peer-to-peer mesh / MCU P2P gives no control on quality, relaying or multi-party (interpreter); an MCU decodes and mixes streams (CPU-heavy, breaks E2EE). The SFU forwards packets: scalable and compatible with E2EE.
E2EE on by default for 1-to-1 Hop-by-hop encryption only Maximum confidentiality for the most sensitive conversations. Cost: no server-side recording or transcription, a little more device CPU.
Chat hot store + archive in the record Chat written directly in the record Low-latency messaging without loading the records store; the record still receives the complete, signed transcript.

2.4 ④ Patient Records Management Service & Emergency Access

Priority Zone Criticality Owns
HIGH — H2 records management · H3 emergency access · H5 integrity · Medium — M4 masking & redaction Clinical Tier 0 (read path, emergency access) · Tier 1 (writes) The medical record (FHIR resources and history), consents, care grants, emergency grants, critical summaries, patient data keys

Mission — keep each patient's lifelong medical record complete, correct and tamper-evident, show it only to the right people for the right reason, and make its critical part available in seconds in an emergency.

Responsibilities

Appendix 1 feature How MedX delivers it
Store and manage medical histories, consultation notes and other records HL7 FHIR R4 resources (conditions, allergies, medications, immunisations, procedures, observations, reports, encounters, clinical notes, documents) stored by a FHIR server (HAPI FHIR on PostgreSQL); binaries in the Secure Document Store.
Allow doctors to add/edit records post-consultation Validated writes with optimistic concurrency; notes are drafts until signed; after signature, changes are addenda (new version with a reason) — the original is never lost. Wrong-patient entries are marked entered-in-error, not deleted.
Give patients access to their records (with restrictions) Patient portal API with patient-scoped tokens; release rules (e.g., results released after doctor review where the law allows), third-party information redacted, proxy scopes, adolescent confidentiality.
Ensure data integrity and regulatory compliance Append-only history, per-patient hash chain anchored daily in WORM storage, provenance on every write, profile validation, full audit of reads and writes, consent registry, retention rules, per-patient encryption and crypto-shredding.
Emergency access (Appendix 2, H3) Dedicated Emergency Access module deployed separately, serving a pre-computed International Patient Summary under a time-boxed break-glass grant — see below.

Clinical data model (FHIR R4)

MedX concept FHIR resource(s) Notes
Patient identity Patient MedX ID + national health identifier (INS) stored encrypted
Medical history Condition, AllergyIntolerance, Procedure, Immunization, FamilyMemberHistory Coded with SNOMED CT / ICD-10
Medications MedicationStatement, MedicationRequest (from Prescription) Coded with ATC and national drug codes
Measurements & results Observation, DiagnosticReport LOINC codes; release rules apply
Consultation Encounter + Composition (clinical note) Composition signed by the author
Documents DocumentReference → binary in the Document Store SHA-256 hash in attachment.hash
Who did what Provenance (every write) · AuditEvent (every access, in the Audit Trail)
Patient choices Consent Sharing, research opt-in, break-glass opt-out where allowed
Emergency summary Composition following the IPS profile Pre-computed projection

Profiles: International Patient Summary (IPS) and national profiles (e.g., FR Core) — validation rejects malformed or uncoded data at write time.

Internal design

Every request crosses the same interceptor chain, so no endpoint can forget a control: authorisation → validation → provenance → encryption → integrity → audit → masking.

Write path, versioning and integrity

  1. Optimistic concurrency — updates must send If-Match: W/"<version>"; a concurrent change returns 412 and the doctor merges — no silent lost update.
  2. Append-only history — every change inserts a new row in resource_history; the database role used by the service has no UPDATE/DELETE privilege on history tables (enforced by grants and triggers).
  3. Signature of notes — Composition.status goes preliminary → final when the author signs; afterwards only addenda are possible (amended, with reason and attestation).
  4. Hash chain per patient — each version stores h(n) = SHA-256( h(n-1) ‖ JCS(resource version) ‖ author ‖ timestamp ) (JCS = RFC 8785 canonical JSON). A nightly job recomputes chains; any break raises a security incident.
  5. Daily anchoring — the Merkle root of all chain heads of the day is signed with an HSM key, timestamped (RFC 3161 qualified timestamp) and written to WORM storage: even a database administrator could not rewrite history without detection.
  6. Provenance — who, when, from which encounter, on whose behalf, and why.
  7. Documents — binaries carry a SHA-256 checksum computed at upload and verified at every download.

Access control

Access path Who Conditions Scope
Self Patient Verified identity Own record, subject to release rules
Proxy Parent / caregiver Delegation from User Management Delegated scope; adolescent-confidential items hidden
Care grant Doctor Created automatically at booking with the patient's consent; valid until 30 days after the consultation; renewable; "treating doctor" designation for long-term follow-up Full record except restricted categories without explicit consent
Patient share Any verified doctor Patient shares the record (e.g., with a specialist) for a chosen period As chosen by the patient
Break-glass Doctor holding emergency_access Emergency declared, step-up MFA, not opted out Read-only, 4 hours, this patient, restricted notes excluded
Pharmacist — No access to the record — only to prescriptions assigned to the pharmacy, through the Prescription service —
MedX staff Support, admins No access to clinical data; privacy officers see audit metadata only —

Sensitivity labels — resources in sensitive categories (mental health, sexual and reproductive health, HIV, genetics, addiction) are labelled restricted and require explicit patient consent to be shared beyond their author.

Patient view restrictions — (1) release rules: a new result can be held until the doctor has reviewed it (configurable per jurisdiction; immediate release where the law requires it, e.g., US information-blocking rules); (2) information about third parties written in a note can be redacted from the patient view; (3) proxies see only their delegated scope.

Data masking & redaction (M4)

The policy engine returns obligations with each decision; a shared masking library applies them to the FHIR response before it leaves the service.

Situation Technique Example
Support agent looks up an account Partial masking +33 6 •• •• •• 42, j•••@g•••.com, no clinical data at all
Pharmacist opens a prescription Field allow-list Name, birth date, prescribed items, prescriber — no diagnosis, no notes
Break-glass access Category exclusion Psychotherapy notes excluded; medications and allergies always shown
Patient portal Release rules + redaction Held results hidden; third-party information redacted
Export / sharing a document Tagged-section redaction; PDF redaction that removes the text layer (not a black box drawn over text) Shared discharge letter without family history
Logs, traces, analytics Never logged; tokenised identifiers; de-identification See §5.7

Emergency access (break-glass)

Principle — in an emergency, access is never blocked by process; it is always answered for afterwards. Pre-approval workflows are too slow when a patient is unconscious; MedX grants immediate, narrow, time-boxed access and makes misuse highly visible and sanctioned.

Aspect Design
Who Verified practitioners holding the emergency_access entitlement (emergency medicine, on-call, EMS), granted by the MedX medical lead and re-certified quarterly.
Identification Exact-match search only (national health identifier, MedX ID, or name + birth date + sex) returning at most three candidates with minimal demographics — no browsing, no wildcard, rate-limited.
Declaration Coded reason (unconscious patient, life-threatening situation, patient unable to communicate…) + free-text justification + accountability statement.
Authentication Step-up MFA if the last strong authentication is older than 15 minutes (passkey or professional smart card).
Grant Read-only, this patient only, 4 hours, renewable with a new justification; issued as a signed emergency grant (JWT bound to the clinician's key) that the regular Records API also accepts for the full record.
Data returned International Patient Summary: allergies & intolerances, active problems, current medications, immunisations, implants & devices, past procedures, blood group, pregnancy status, advance directives, emergency contacts. The full record is available under the same grant, restricted notes excluded.
Patient choice Patients can opt out of break-glass where the law allows it (warned about the risk); where it does not, the flag is ignored.
Accountability AuditEvent with purposeOfUse = ETREAT written in the same transaction as the grant (no access without audit); real-time SIEM alert to the privacy office; patient notified (in-app + e-mail) within 24 h with who/when/what; mandatory review within 72 h by the privacy officer and a medical lead; unjustified use → suspension and referral to the professional body; behaviour analytics flag outliers.

Why it keeps working when the rest is degraded (Tier 0)

Failure Effect on emergency access
Records primary database down None — summaries are read from replicas; grants are written in the Emergency Access service's own database.
Primary region lost None beyond DNS failover — the Emergency Access API is active in the DR region with its own grant database and local replicas (lag < 1 s).
Event bus / audit pipeline down None — audit events wait in the outbox and are delivered later; nothing is lost.
Policy bundle server down None — OPA sidecars keep the last signed bundle.
Identity provider slow Clinicians with a recent strong authentication proceed; tokens are validated locally with cached keys. The IdP itself is active in both regions.
Traffic spike on the rest of MedX None — separate deployment with reserved capacity (bulkhead) and its own rate limits.

Performance — the critical summary is a pre-computed projection refreshed within seconds of any change (event-driven), stored as one encrypted row per patient: one indexed read from the nearest replica, one cached key unwrap, one decryption → p95 < 300 ms.

API (selection)

Method Endpoint Purpose
GET /fhir/Patient/{id}/$summary IPS summary (patient, care team)
GET /fhir/{type}?patient={id}&… FHIR search
POST / PUT /fhir/{type} · /fhir/{type}/{id} Create / update (If-Match required)
GET /fhir/{type}/{id}/_history Version history
POST /fhir/Composition/{id}/$sign Sign a clinical note
GET /fhir/Patient/{id}/$everything Full export (right of access / portability) — FHIR bundle or PDF
POST /v1/emergency-access/requests Break-glass request → grant + critical summary
GET /v1/patients/me/access-log "Who accessed my record" (from the audit trail)
PUT /v1/patients/me/consents/{type} Sharing, research, break-glass opt-out

Events

  • Publishes records.record.v1 (RecordUpdated, DocumentAdded, ResultReleased, ConsentChanged) and records.emergency.v1 (BreakGlassGranted, BreakGlassReviewDue, BreakGlassReviewed).
  • Consumes identity.user.v1 (create patient record and data keys; revoke grants of suspended practitioners), scheduling.appointment.v1 (create/revoke care grants), consultation.session.v1 (Encounter, chat transcript archive), prescription.v1 (medication list and summary refresh).

Data owned

PostgreSQL records database: resource (current versions, JSONB, sensitive elements encrypted), resource_history (append-only, hash chain), search-parameter indexes, care_grant, consent, critical_summary, patient_key (wrapped data keys), outbox. Emergency Access has its own small database (emergency_grant, review_case, outbox). Binaries in the Document Store. Details in §3.4.

Scalability & resilience

  • Read-heavy (≈ 5–10 reads per write; ≈ 600 reads/s at Year-3 peak): a synchronous standby and two read replicas across the three AZs, plus replicas in the DR region; read-your-writes guaranteed for the author by routing their reads to the primary for a few seconds after a write.
  • UI screens read the patient timeline projection (one query per screen) instead of assembling many FHIR searches.
  • Growth path: table partitioning by patient hash from day one; if write throughput ever exceeds one primary, shard by patient_id (e.g., Citus) — almost every query is patient-scoped, so shards stay independent.
  • No PHI in shared caches; the only cache of clinical data is the encrypted critical summary.

Design decisions & trade-offs

Decision Alternative Why this choice
FHIR R4 as the internal model (HAPI FHIR on PostgreSQL) Custom relational schema Interoperability (national services, hospitals), built-in validation, versioning and search; hiring and audit are easier. Cost: generic storage is less efficient → projections for UI screens.
Append-only history + hash chain + anchoring In-place updates with an audit table Integrity is a High priority: history cannot be rewritten silently, even by an administrator. Cost: storage growth (≈ +30 %), acceptable.
Break-glass with post-hoc review Pre-approval by a supervisor Minutes matter in an emergency; deterrence (audit, alerts, notice to patient, review, sanctions) controls misuse.
Per-patient encryption keys Database encryption only A leaked backup, replica or query result is useless without KMS; crypto-shredding at end of retention. Cost: key management and ~1 ms per request with key caching.
Separate Emergency Access deployment and database Endpoint of the main Records API Isolation from load and failures of the main API; can run active in two regions. Cost: one more deployable unit.

2.5 ⑤ Prescription Management Service

Priority Zone Criticality Owns
Medium — M3 prescription management Clinical Tier 1 Prescriptions and their versions, signatures, safety-check results, fulfilment status, renewal requests

Mission — turn a doctor's decision into a safe, signed, verifiable electronic prescription that reaches the right pharmacy in seconds, can be corrected or revoked instantly, and whose progress the patient can follow.

Responsibilities

Appendix 1 feature How MedX delivers it
Doctors create, modify or revoke prescriptions post-consultation Draft within an encounter → automatic safety checks → e-signature (step-up MFA) → active. Modification creates a new signed version that supersedes the previous one; revocation is a signed status change with a reason.
Notify pharmacies of new prescriptions or changes PrescriptionIssued / Modified / Revoked events → Pharmacy Interface pushes to the pharmacy inbox and PMS webhook; revocations are critical (multi-channel, escalated until acknowledged).
Enable patients to view active prescriptions Patient API and app screen: active prescriptions, remaining renewals, validity dates, printable PDF with QR code.
Track prescription fulfilment status Fulfilment state machine fed by pharmacy updates; each change is visible to the patient and the prescriber.

Prescription and fulfilment lifecycles

The legal status of the prescription and the fulfilment status at the pharmacy are two separate state machines — mixing them is a classic source of errors (e.g., "ready for pickup" on a revoked prescription).

Partial dispensing and renewals are tracked per line item (dispensed_quantity, refills_remaining).

Creating and signing a prescription

  • Safety checks (clinical decision support): drug–drug interactions, allergy and cross-allergy, duplicate therapy, contraindications (pregnancy, age, renal function when known), dose range. The call to Records uses token exchange (RFC 8693) so the request is authorised as the doctor, not as a privileged service. If a check is unavailable, the doctor is told so explicitly and must acknowledge before signing.
  • Signature: the canonical prescription (RFC 8785 JSON) is signed with the prescriber's key, held in the HSM and usable only after a fresh MFA; alternatively a qualified signature from a trust service provider or the professional smart card (eIDAS). The signed version is immutable.
  • QR code / verification code: lets a pharmacy verify authenticity and current status (not revoked, not already dispensed, not expired) — it does not contain the prescription content.

Modify and revoke

Action Rules Pharmacy side
Modify Only if not fully dispensed. Creates version n+1 (new signature) referencing version n, which becomes Superseded; dispensed quantities stay valid. PrescriptionModified (high priority); if preparation had started, the pharmacist must acknowledge the change before continuing.
Revoke Reason required (error, adverse reaction, change of treatment). Signed status change. PrescriptionRevoked (critical): portal alert + PMS webhook; if not acknowledged within 15 min, SMS/phone escalation to the pharmacy. If already dispensed, the prescriber is alerted to contact the patient.
Renew Patient requests a renewal from the app → task for the prescriber → new prescription linked to the previous one, or refusal with a message. New PrescriptionIssued.

Controlled substances follow stricter, configurable rules per jurisdiction (secure prescription requirements, maximum durations, no remote renewal, additional identity checks at the pharmacy).

API (selection)

Method Endpoint Purpose
POST /v1/prescriptions Create a draft (encounter, items)
POST /v1/prescriptions/{id}/checks Run / re-run safety checks
POST /v1/prescriptions/{id}/sign Sign (step-up MFA) → Active
POST /v1/prescriptions/{id}/versions Modify → new signed version
POST /v1/prescriptions/{id}/revoke Revoke with reason
PUT /v1/prescriptions/{id}/pharmacy Patient assigns or changes the pharmacy
GET /v1/patients/me/prescriptions?status=active Patient view
GET /v1/prescriptions/{id}/fulfilment Fulfilment status timeline
GET /v1/prescriptions/verify?code= Pharmacy verification (authenticity + status)
GET /fhir/MedicationRequest?patient= Interoperability view

Events

  • Publishes prescription.v1: PrescriptionIssued, PrescriptionModified, PrescriptionRevoked, PrescriptionExpired, PharmacyAssigned, FulfilmentStatusChanged.
  • Consumes pharmacy.fulfilment.v1 (acknowledgements and status updates, idempotent by sequence number), identity.user.v1 (a suspended prescriber can no longer sign; active prescriptions are flagged for review).

Data owned

PostgreSQL: prescription, prescription_version (signed, immutable), prescription_item (drug code, structured dosage, quantity, refills, substitution allowed), signature, status_history (append-only), fulfilment, safety_check (warnings and overrides with reason), renewal_request, outbox. Drug reference data is a read-only replica refreshed from the drug database (public reference data, not PHI). Details in §3.4.

Security & privacy

  • Signing requires a fresh strong authentication; signing keys never leave the HSM.
  • Minimum necessary for pharmacies: patient name, birth date, (insurance number where required), items, prescriber identity and signature — never diagnosis or notes.
  • Every read by a pharmacy is audited; verification endpoint rate-limited against enumeration of codes.

Scalability & resilience

  • 120 k prescriptions/day at Year 3 (≈ 1.4/s average, ≈ 15/s peak) plus ≈ 5 status updates each — light load; the service scales horizontally and the drug search is cached.
  • Revocation delivery is designed for safety, not throughput: outbox (no lost event), push + webhook + escalation, and a reconciliation job that compares prescription and pharmacy states every 5 minutes.

Design decisions & trade-offs

Decision Alternative Why this choice
Modification = new signed version Edit in place Legal traceability: the pharmacy and the auditor can always see what was signed, when, and what replaced it.
Separate legal status and fulfilment status One status field Prevents contradictory states; each has a single owner (prescriber vs pharmacy).
FHIR MedicationRequest / MedicationDispense / Task mapping Proprietary format Direct path to national e-prescription services: where such a service exists (e.g., France's ordonnance numérique), an adapter registers each prescription there and the national service becomes the reference for dispensing.
Allergy check via Records at signing time Local copy of allergies Always current data for a safety decision; failure is explicit, never silent.

2.6 ⑥ Pharmacy Interface Service

Priority Zone Criticality Owns
Low — L1 pharmacy interface Clinical (minimised prescription data) Tier 2 Pharmacy registry, integrations, fulfilment tasks, patient–pharmacy conversations, inventory availability cache

Mission — connect every pharmacy, from the independent shop with a web browser to the chain with its own pharmacy management system (PMS), to MedX prescriptions — reliably and with the minimum patient data.

Responsibilities

Appendix 1 feature How MedX delivers it
Confirm prescription receipt and update statuses ("Ready for pickup", "Dispatched"…) Real-time inbox (portal) or webhook + partner API (PMS); acknowledgement with SLA tracking; status updates validated against the fulfilment state machine and forwarded to the Prescription service.
Interaction between patients and pharmacies Secure conversation threads attached to a prescription (availability questions, substitution proposals, pickup times), with notifications on both sides and message templates.
Integrate with inventory systems Inventory adapters per PMS vendor behind a common availability port; cached availability levels; "find a pharmacy that has my medicine nearby".

Integration modes

Mode For whom Details
Pharmacy portal Every pharmacy, no integration needed Web app with real-time inbox, prescription view and printing, QR-code scan (webcam) for verification, status buttons, conversations.
Partner API + webhooks Pharmacies whose PMS vendor integrates REST and FHIR (Task, MedicationDispense) API; OAuth 2.0 client credentials with mTLS-bound tokens; outbound webhooks signed (HMAC-SHA256 + timestamp) with replay protection, retries with exponential backoff for 24 h, then dead-letter and portal fallback.
Inventory adapters Pharmacies sharing stock data Common port checkAvailability(pharmacy, items) returning IN_STOCK, LOW, OUT_OF_STOCK or UNKNOWN; strategies: push of stock deltas, real-time pull (2–3 s timeout) or nightly batch, depending on the vendor.

Fulfilment flow

  • Unable to fulfil (out of stock, substitution refused): the patient is notified and offered nearby pharmacies that report the medicine in stock; reassignment restarts the flow.
  • Unacknowledged prescriptions: if the SLA is missed, the patient is told and can choose another pharmacy.
  • Status updates are idempotent: each update carries a sequence number; duplicates and out-of-order webhook retries are ignored.

Data minimisation

A pharmacy only ever sees prescriptions assigned to it (or presented by the patient via the QR code), and only the fields needed to dispense: patient name, birth date, insurance number where required, items, prescriber identity and signature. No diagnosis, no consultation notes, no record access. Inventory data is exposed to patients as availability levels, not quantities (commercial confidentiality).

API (selection)

Method Endpoint Purpose
GET /v1/pharmacy/inbox?status= Pharmacy inbox
POST /v1/pharmacy/fulfilments/{id}/acknowledge Confirm receipt
POST /v1/pharmacy/fulfilments/{id}/status Update status (sequence number, idempotent)
POST /v1/pharmacy/fulfilments/{id}/dispense Record dispensed items and quantities
GET /v1/pharmacies/search?lat=&lon=&item= Nearby pharmacies with availability (patient)
POST /v1/conversations · /v1/conversations/{id}/messages Patient–pharmacy conversation
GET /partner/fhir/Task?owner={pharmacy}&status=requested PMS pull mode
POST /partner/v1/fulfilments/{id}/status PMS status push

Events

  • Publishes pharmacy.fulfilment.v1: FulfilmentAcknowledged, FulfilmentStatusUpdated, UnableToFulfil, InquiryMessagePosted.
  • Consumes prescription.v1: Issued, Modified, Revoked, PharmacyAssigned.

Data owned

PostgreSQL: pharmacy (registry number, address, geolocation, opening hours, services), integration (mode, endpoint, credential references in Vault), fulfilment_task, status_event (append-only), conversation, message (encrypted), outbox. Redis: availability cache. Geo search with PostGIS. Details in §3.4.

Scalability & resilience

  • 15 k pharmacies, ≈ 600 k status updates/day at Year 3 (≈ 7/s): light; webhook delivery workers scale on queue lag.
  • A slow or failing PMS never blocks MedX: webhooks are asynchronous with retries and dead-letter, and the portal is always available as a fallback.
  • Inventory queries are cached (15 min) and time-boxed; "unknown" is an acceptable answer.

Design decisions & trade-offs

Decision Alternative Why this choice
Portal and API API only Inclusion: small pharmacies can join on day one; integrated ones get automation. Cost: two channels to maintain.
Adapter per PMS vendor behind one port Force one format on all vendors Vendors integrate at their own pace; MedX's core stays clean (anti-corruption layer).
Availability levels, not quantities Exact stock Enough for the patient's decision; protects pharmacies' commercial data.
Low priority, delivered after the clinical core Early delivery Follows MedX priorities; until then, prescriptions are printable with a verifiable QR code usable in any pharmacy.

2.7 ⑦ Notification Service

Priority Zone Criticality Owns
Low — L2 preferences (applied) · L3 delivery & read tracking — a minimal version ships with the Medium features (booking confirmations, reminders) Engagement (no PHI) Tier 2 (critical messages have their own lane) Templates, local replica of preferences, notification log, delivery statuses, in-app inbox

Mission — tell the right person the right thing on the right channel at the right time, without ever putting health information in an SMS, an e-mail or a push banner.

Responsibilities

Appendix 1 feature How MedX delivers it
Send alerts, reminders, updates (SMS, e-mail, in-app) Event-driven pipeline with channel workers for SMS, e-mail, push (APNs/FCM) and in-app (Real-time Gateway + inbox); two providers per external channel with automatic failover.
Handle notification preferences (opt-in/opt-out, frequency) Preferences owned by User Management and replicated locally from PreferencesUpdated; evaluated per category × channel, with quiet hours, frequency caps and digests.
Track delivery and read status Status machine fed by provider receipts and client read receipts, stored in an append-only notification log; bounce handling; delivery dashboards.

Pipeline

Priority lanes

Lane Examples Behaviour Target
P0 critical Prescription revoked (to the pharmacy), urgent consultation assigned (to a doctor), break-glass alert (to the privacy office) Ignores quiet hours; several channels in parallel; escalation if not read (e.g., SMS after 5 min, then phone) dispatched < 10 s
P1 transactional Booking confirmation or change, reminders, "medicine ready", payment receipt Mandatory category (channel can be chosen, not disabled) dispatched < 60 s
P2 informational New document or message available Fully controlled by preferences; digest possible < 5 min
P3 marketing Newsletter, surveys Explicit opt-in only (GDPR/ePrivacy), frequency caps batch

Each lane has its own Kafka topic and worker pool, so a burst of reminders can never delay a revocation alert.

PHI-safe content

Channel Example of what MedX sends What it never contains
SMS "MedX: your teleconsultation is tomorrow at 10:30. Join from the app." Doctor name or specialty, reason, drug names, results
E-mail Generic subject, deep link to the app, sender authentication (SPF, DKIM, DMARC) Attachments with health data (invoices and documents are downloaded in the app)
Push "You have a new message" Message content on the lock screen
In-app Full details after authentication —

Templates can only use allow-listed variables; a CI check rejects any template referencing a clinical field.

Preferences

  • Owned and edited in User Management (single source of truth); replicated here through PreferencesUpdated events into a local table and a Redis cache → no synchronous dependency at send time.
  • Evaluated per category × channel (appointments, prescriptions, documents, messages, marketing), with quiet hours in the user's time zone, frequency caps (e.g., max 3 non-critical SMS per day) and daily digests.
  • Mandatory notifications (security, legal, P0/P1) cannot be switched off entirely, only routed.

Delivery and read tracking (L3)

  • Status events are appended (never updated in place) with provider references and timestamps.
  • No tracking pixels in e-mails (privacy): "read" for e-mail means a link was clicked or the item was opened in the app.
  • Hard bounces mark the contact point invalid and emit ContactPointInvalid so the user is asked to update it.
  • Dashboards: delivery rate per channel and provider, latency per lane; alert when a provider degrades (automatic failover to the second provider).

Reliability

  • Idempotency: deduplication key = event ID + recipient + channel (Redis, 24 h) — replays never double-send.
  • Retries with exponential backoff and jitter, provider failover, dead-letter queue with operator replay.
  • Reminder batches (e.g., all 9:00 appointments) are spread with jitter across the sending window.

API (selection)

Method Endpoint Purpose
POST /v1/notifications Internal ad hoc send (service-to-service only)
GET /v1/users/me/notifications?cursor= In-app inbox
POST /v1/users/me/notifications/{id}/read Read receipt
POST /v1/webhooks/providers/{provider} Delivery receipts (signature verified)
GET /v1/admin/notifications/metrics Delivery statistics (aggregated, no content)

Events

  • Consumes almost every business topic (see the event catalogue) and identity.preferences.v1.
  • Publishes notification.delivery.v1: NotificationSent, NotificationDelivered, NotificationRead, NotificationFailed, ContactPointInvalid.

Data owned

PostgreSQL: template (versioned, per locale), preference_replica, provider_config. Cassandra: notification_by_recipient (partition = recipient + month), notification_status_event, TTL 13 months. Redis: deduplication keys, frequency counters, rate limits. Details in §3.4.

Scalability & resilience

  • 2 M notifications/day at Year 3 (≈ 25/s average, ≈ 500/s at reminder peaks): Kafka absorbs bursts; workers autoscale on consumer lag per lane; providers are rate-limited per account.
  • Cassandra handles the write-heavy log (≈ 4 status events per notification) linearly, with TTL-based expiry instead of costly deletes.

Design decisions & trade-offs

Decision Alternative Why this choice
Generic, PHI-free external messages Rich messages ("your dermatology appointment…") SMS and e-mail are neither private nor within the HDS scope; convenience is kept by deep links into the authenticated app.
Wide-column store (Cassandra) for the log PostgreSQL Append-heavy time series queried by recipient, with TTL expiry: a natural fit; PostgreSQL stays for templates and preferences.
Build the orchestrator, buy the channels Notification SaaS for everything Preference, PHI and priority rules are MedX-specific and sensitive; message delivery is a commodity.
Separate lanes per priority One queue Guarantees that critical safety messages are never stuck behind bulk reminders.

2.8 ⑧ Billing & Payment Service

Priority Zone Criticality Owns
Low — L5 secure payment · L6 refunds Payment (PCI scope minimised) Tier 2 Prices, payments (PSP references), double-entry ledger, invoices and credit notes, refunds, payouts

Mission — charge the right amount at the right time, never touch a card number, keep books that reconcile to the cent, and refund quickly and traceably when something goes wrong.

Responsibilities

Appendix 1 feature How MedX delivers it
Handle consultation fees and process payments Price per practitioner and consultation type; pre-authorisation at booking, capture after the consultation; cancellation policy; marketplace payouts to practitioners and pharmacies through the PSP.
Generate invoices for consultations and medication Invoice issued on capture (on behalf of the practitioner or pharmacy): gapless numbering per issuer, immutable PDF stored WORM, no clinical detail on the invoice.
Process refunds if necessary Automatic (doctor cancels, consultation failed technically) or manual (support within a threshold, 4-eyes above it); credit notes; full ledger trace.
Provide secure transaction mechanisms PSP hosted payment fields (card data never reaches MedX) → PCI DSS SAQ A; 3-D Secure 2 (PSD2 strong customer authentication); tokenised payment methods; signed webhooks; idempotency everywhere.

Payment lifecycle

  • Authorisation expiry — card authorisations expire after about 7 days, so for appointments booked further ahead the card is saved with strong authentication (setup intent) and authorised automatically 24 h before.
  • Cancellation policy — free until 24 h before; late cancellation or no-show fee as disclosed at booking; doctor cancellation or technical failure → automatic full release/refund.
  • Medication charges — when a pharmacy offers delivery or click-and-collect with online payment, the order is paid through the same flow; the invoice is issued on behalf of the pharmacy.
  • Payouts — marketplace accounts at the PSP split each payment between the practitioner or pharmacy and the MedX fee; the PSP performs the payees' identity checks (KYC).

Refunds (L6)

Ledger and reconciliation

  • Double-entry, append-only ledger: every money movement is a balanced journal entry (patient receivable, practitioner/pharmacy payable, MedX revenue, PSP clearing, refunds). Entries are never updated — corrections are new entries.
  • Idempotency: every PSP call carries an idempotency key; every PSP webhook is de-duplicated by event ID and its raw payload kept for audit.
  • Daily reconciliation with the PSP settlement report; any difference opens an incident.
  • Invoices are immutable; a refund produces a credit note, never an edited invoice. Retention 10 years (commercial law), WORM storage.

PCI DSS scope minimisation

Measure Effect
PSP-hosted fields / drop-in components (iframes) in the apps Card numbers go from the device straight to the PSP; MedX stores only tokens, brand and last 4 digits.
Payment page script integrity (CSP, SRI, change detection — PCI DSS v4 req. 6.4.3 and 11.6.1) Protects the page that embeds the PSP component against script injection (e-skimming).
Restricted PSP API keys in Vault, rotated A leaked key cannot read card data or move funds beyond its permissions.
Payment namespace isolated by network policy Only Scheduling, the gateway (webhooks) and the event bus can reach Billing.
No PHI in billing Invoices say "Teleconsultation", never a specialty or a diagnosis.

API (selection)

Method Endpoint Purpose
POST /v1/payment-methods/setup Returns a PSP client secret for the hosted fields
POST /v1/payments/authorizations Internal (Scheduling): authorise a fee
POST /v1/payments/{id}/capture Internal: capture after the consultation
POST /v1/refunds Request a refund (automatic rules, support agent)
POST /v1/refunds/{id}/approve Second approval above threshold
GET /v1/users/me/invoices · /v1/invoices/{id}/pdf Patient invoices
POST /v1/webhooks/psp PSP events (signature verified, deduplicated)

Events

  • Publishes billing.payment.v1: PaymentAuthorized, PaymentFailed, PaymentCaptured, PaymentVoided, RefundSucceeded, RefundFailed, InvoiceIssued.
  • Consumes consultation.session.v1 (capture or refund), scheduling.appointment.v1 (cancellations, no-shows), pharmacy.fulfilment.v1 (paid medication orders).

Data owned

PostgreSQL: customer (PSP customer reference), payment_method (token, brand, last 4), payment, ledger_account, journal_entry + journal_line (append-only), invoice + invoice_line, credit_note, refund, psp_event (raw, deduplication), payout, outbox. Amounts stored as integers in minor units + ISO 4217 currency. Invoice PDFs in the Document Store (WORM). Details in §3.4.

Scalability & resilience

  • ≈ 200 k payments/day at Year 3 (≈ 2–3/s): throughput is not the challenge, correctness is — hence idempotency, outbox, ledger and reconciliation.
  • If the PSP is unavailable, bookings can proceed in "pay later" mode (configurable by risk), captured when the PSP recovers; no request is lost thanks to the outbox and retries.

Design decisions & trade-offs

Decision Alternative Why this choice
PSP hosted fields (SAQ A) Handle card data (SAQ D) Removes the heaviest compliance scope and the most attractive target. Cost: less control of the payment UI.
Own double-entry ledger Rely on the PSP dashboard Auditability, marketplace splits, refunds and reconciliation require MedX's own books.
Pre-authorise then capture Charge at booking Patient pays only for consultations that happened; fewer refunds. Cost: authorisation-expiry handling.
Low priority, but security by design from day one Postpone security with the feature Payment is delivered last, but its design already keeps card data out of MedX.

2.9 Platform Components

Shared capabilities used by every business service. Several of them carry High-priority requirements (H1 encryption, H4 authorization, H5 integrity and secure files), so they are built once, by the platform team, and reused everywhere.

Component Priority served Tier
API Gateway & edge H1, H4 0
Real-time Gateway M2 1
Policy Decision Point (OPA) H4, M4 0
Event bus (Kafka) & outbox H5 1
Secure Document Store H1, H5 1
Audit Trail H2, H3, H5 1 (writes buffered in outboxes)
Keys & secrets H1 0
Observability & security monitoring all 1
De-identified data platform L4 2

API Gateway & edge

  • CDN serves only static assets (app bundles, images); API responses containing personal data are sent with Cache-Control: no-store and never cached at the edge.
  • WAF with OWASP core rules, bot management, geo/IP reputation, virtual patching; DDoS protection L3–L7.
  • API Gateway (Envoy-based): TLS 1.3 termination (HSTS), routing by audience (/patient, /clinician, /pharmacy, /partner; /admin is not exposed publicly — reachable only through the zero-trust access proxy), JWT validation for three issuers (realms) with cached JWKS, DPoP proof validation, mTLS for partners, per-user / per-IP / per-client rate limits and quotas (stricter on login, search and verification endpoints), request size limits, OpenAPI schema validation, CORS, security headers, correlation IDs, webhook ingress per provider with signature verification.
  • Access logs contain metadata only (route, status, latency, pseudonymous subject) — never bodies or query strings with personal data.

Real-time Gateway

  • WebSocket (WSS) connections for chat, presence, live statuses and in-app notifications — one connection per app, multiplexing channels.
  • Authentication at connection time (access token); every channel subscription (user:{id}, consultation:{id}, pharmacy:{id}) is authorised by the owning service; connections are re-validated on token refresh and closed on revocation.
  • Stateless fan-out through Redis pub/sub (or NATS): any node can deliver to any user; heartbeats, resume tokens after reconnect, connection draining on deployment.
  • Sizing: 200 k concurrent connections at Year 3 peak ≈ 10 pods at ~25 k connections each, autoscaled on connection count.

Policy Decision Point (OPA)

  • Sidecar next to every service: decisions in < 1 ms, no network hop, keeps working if the policy server is down.
  • Policies written in Rego, stored in Git, reviewed, unit-tested in CI (positive and negative cases for every rule), compiled into signed bundles, distributed to sidecars (pull every 60 s, last good bundle kept).
  • Inputs: subject (from the validated token), action, resource (type, owner patient, security labels), purpose of use, and per-request facts looked up by the service (care grant, consent, emergency grant).
  • Outputs: allow + obligations (masking, exclusions, audit level).
  • Decision logs (without PHI) go to the audit pipeline for forensics.

Event bus (Kafka) & outbox

  • No dual writes: an event exists if and only if the business change was committed.
  • Kafka: 3 brokers over 3 AZs, replication factor 3, min.insync.replicas = 2, acks = all, idempotent producers; TLS + SASL/mTLS authentication, ACLs per service (a service can only produce its own topics and consume what it needs), encryption at rest.
  • Schema registry with backward-compatibility checks in CI; breaking changes = new topic version.
  • Retention 7 days (30 days for audit.events.v1); dead-letter topic per consumer group with alerting and replay.

Secure Document Store

  • Double encryption: application-level AES-256-GCM with a per-file data key (wrapped by the Documents KEK and registered against the owner patient for crypto-shredding) plus bucket-level SSE-KMS.
  • Integrity: SHA-256 computed by the client, verified at upload, re-verified at every download and by a weekly scrub job; object versioning; Object Lock (compliance mode) for documents under legal retention.
  • Access: downloads go through the Document Store, which asks the owning service's policy (Records, Consultation, Billing) whether the caller may read this document; streamed decryption; every download audited. Quarantine objects are deleted after 24 h at the latest.
  • Limits: 50 MB per file; allowed types PDF, JPEG, PNG, HEIC (DICOM imaging is out of scope for v1).
  • Durability: object storage durability of 11 nines + cross-region replication + immutable backup copy.

Audit Trail

  • What is audited: every read, creation, update, export, sharing, break-glass, authentication event and administrative action on personal data. Schema aligned with FHIR AuditEvent / IHE BALP: who (subject, role, organisation, assurance level, device, IP), what (action, resource type/ID, patient), when, why (purpose of use: treatment, emergency treatment, patient request, payment, operations, support), outcome, correlation ID.
  • Pipeline: services write audit events to their outbox in the same transaction as the access → Kafka audit.events.v1 (restricted ACL) → Audit service → (1) WORM archive: batches hash-chained, Merkle root signed by an HSM key and timestamped daily, stored with Object Lock in the security account; (2) search index (restricted OpenSearch, 13 months) for investigations and for the patient's "who accessed my record" page; (3) SIEM stream for real-time rules.
  • Who can read it: privacy officers and auditors (read-only, themselves audited); patients see their own access history; no engineer can modify or delete audit data.
  • Retention: at least 6 years, configurable up to the medical-record retention.

Keys & secrets

  • KMS backed by HSMs (FIPS 140-3 level 3): key-encryption keys per service × environment × data class; usage restricted by IAM policy (the Billing role cannot decrypt Records keys); automatic yearly rotation; multi-region keys for DR; every use logged.
  • Envelope encryption in the services (see §5.6): per-patient / per-file / per-consultation data keys, cached unwrapped in memory ≤ 5 min.
  • HashiCorp Vault: dynamic database credentials (1 h TTL), Transit engine for encrypting integration secrets (calendar OAuth tokens, PMS credentials), PKI for internal certificates, secrets injected at runtime — no secret in code, images or plain environment variables; separation of duties between key custodians and data administrators.

Observability & security monitoring

  • OpenTelemetry everywhere: traces (W3C traceparent propagated through HTTP and Kafka headers), metrics (RED for services, USE for resources), structured logs. Backends: Prometheus/Grafana, Loki, Tempo.
  • PHI never in telemetry: log fields are allow-listed, identifiers tokenised, request bodies never logged; a scanner samples logs for PHI patterns and alerts.
  • SLOs and error budgets per service tier; multi-window burn-rate alerts; synthetic probes call the emergency path every minute from both regions.
  • SIEM correlation rules: break-glass events, mass record access, access without care grant attempts, impossible travel, MFA disabled, privilege escalation, anomalous exports; user and entity behaviour analytics to detect "curious insiders" (e.g., a doctor opening records of patients with no appointment, or of a celebrity).

De-identified data platform

  • Purpose: product analytics, capacity planning, quality indicators, research (with consent), and datasets for staging, demo and tests (L4).
  • Change-data-capture from service replicas into a secure processing enclave in the production account, where pseudonymisation/anonymisation jobs run; only de-identified outputs leave the enclave (columnar files queried by an analytics engine).
  • Techniques and controls are described in §5.7: removal of direct identifiers, keyed pseudonyms, generalisation, date shifting, k-anonymity checks, DPO approval.
  • Staging and demo use synthetic patients (e.g., generated with Synthea in FHIR format) — never real PHI.

3. Data Model & Storage Strategy

Deliverable 3. Synthetic analysis of the data model and of the storage chosen for each component. Component behaviour is described in 2. Detailed component designs.

3.1 Principles

  1. Database per service. Each service owns its schema, credentials and migrations; no other service reads its tables. Cross-service references are identifiers only (UUIDv7), resolved through APIs or events.
  2. PostgreSQL by default. Transactions, constraints, JSONB, mature replication and point-in-time recovery, a managed Multi-AZ offering inside the HDS scope, and skills that are easy to hire. A specialised store is added only when it solves a problem PostgreSQL does not solve well (§3.3).
  3. Classify before storing. Every field has a data class (§3.2) that decides its encryption, masking, logging and retention rules.
  4. Append-only for anything clinical, legal or financial. Records, prescriptions, fulfilment statuses, ledger and audit are never updated in place — changes are new versions or new entries.
  5. Derived data is disposable. Caches, search indexes and projections can be rebuilt from the systems of record; they are never the only copy of anything.
  6. Every store is encrypted, private, backed up, monitored and has a retention rule — no exception.

3.2 Data classification

Class Definition Examples Mandatory controls
C4 — Sensitive health data Clinical content, sensitive categories, national health identifier Notes, diagnoses, results, documents, chat content, mental/sexual health, genetics, INS Clinical zone only · per-patient application encryption + storage encryption · ABAC with purpose of use · never cached (except encrypted emergency summary) · never in logs, events, search indexes or non-prod
C3 — Health-related personal data Data revealing that a person receives care Appointments, doctor–patient links, prescriptions, fulfilment statuses Clinical zone · storage encryption, sensitive fields encrypted · minimised for pharmacies · audited access
C2 — Personal data Identity and contact data without health information Name, e-mail, phone, address, preferences, invoices Field encryption for contact data · masking for support · GDPR rights applied
C1 — Internal Operational, non-personal Configuration, metrics, pseudonymous telemetry Access control, standard encryption
C0 — Public Meant to be published Doctor public profiles, drug reference data, static content Integrity controls

3.3 Storage technology choices

Technology Role at MedX Chosen because Deliberately not used for
PostgreSQL (managed, Multi-AZ, synchronous standby, read replicas, cross-region replica) System of record of all eight services, the FHIR store, emergency grants, document metadata ACID, rich constraints (e.g., exclusion constraint against double booking), JSONB for FHIR resources, row-level security, PITR, mature HA Very high-volume append-only logs with TTL (chat hot store, notification log)
Redis / Valkey (cluster, replicas in 3 AZs, TLS, encryption at rest) Slot holds, availability cache, sessions and token denylist, rate limits, idempotency keys, presence, pub/sub Sub-millisecond latency, atomic SET NX, TTLs, pub/sub Any source of truth (everything in Redis can be rebuilt)
Cassandra (RF 3 across 3 AZs, TLS, encryption at rest) Consultation chat hot store (30 days), notification log (13 months) Linear write scalability, time-ordered partitions, native TTL, multi-datacenter replication Relational integrity, ad hoc queries, long-term clinical storage
Object storage (S3-compatible: versioning, Object Lock, SSE-KMS, cross-region replication) Medical documents, chat transcripts, prescription PDFs, invoices, audit archive, backups 11-nines durability, WORM retention, lifecycle tiers, low cost at 150 TB Small structured records
OpenSearch (private, encrypted, fine-grained access control) Doctor directory, drug catalogue search, restricted audit investigation index Full-text, facets, geo queries, fast aggregation Storing clinical content (it is not a PHI store)
Kafka (3 brokers, RF 3) Event log, 7 days (30 days for audit) Durable, ordered per key, replayable Long-term storage
Columnar analytics store (Parquet files + query engine) De-identified analytics Cheap scans over large volumes Identifiable data

Alternatives considered — a document database for FHIR JSON (PostgreSQL JSONB gives the same flexibility with cross-resource transactions and one less technology to secure); a ledger database for audit (hash-chained batches on WORM object storage give tamper evidence without a niche product); DynamoDB-style key-value stores (vendor lock-in and harder portability across HDS providers).

Cross-service domain model

Entities belong to one service; relationships across services are references by identifier.

Entity Owner service Store
Patient, Practitioner, Pharmacy (identity, organisation) ① User Management PostgreSQL
Appointment ② Scheduling PostgreSQL

Medical record, Encounter, clinical resources ④ Patient Records PostgreSQL (FHIR)

① User Management

Blind index: email_blind_index = HMAC-SHA256(k, normalised e-mail) lets the service find an account by e-mail without storing the address in clear; the HMAC key lives in Vault.

② Scheduling

The exclusion constraint on (practitioner_id, tstzrange(starts_at, ends_at)) for active statuses is described in §2.2. Redis keys: hold:{practitioner}:{start} (TTL 10 min), avail:{practitioner}:{date} (hash of free slots), waitlist:{practitioner|specialty} (sorted set by urgency then time).

③ Consultation

Cassandra partition = consultation_id (all messages of one consultation together, ordered by timeuuid); default_time_to_live = 30 days; the transcript is archived into the record before expiry.

④ Patient Records and Emergency Access

  • RESOURCE.content holds the FHIR JSON; elements classified C4 (free-text notes, sensitive categories, national identifier) are replaced by ciphertext encrypted with the patient key (AES-256-GCM, additional authenticated data = resource ID + version, so ciphertext cannot be moved to another resource).
  • FHIR search parameters are extracted into indexed tables at write time (as HAPI FHIR does) — only non-sensitive search parameters (codes, dates, statuses) are indexed in clear.
  • Tables are partitioned by hash of patient_id from day one, preparing for sharding by patient.
  • The database role of the service has INSERT/SELECT only on RESOURCE_HISTORY; a trigger rejects any update.

⑤ Prescription

⑥ Pharmacy Interface

⑦ Notification (Cassandra)

Query-driven tables: "a user's notifications, newest first" and "the status history of one notification".

CREATE TABLE notification_by_recipient (

⑧ Billing & Payment

Invariant enforced by a deferred constraint trigger: for every JOURNAL_ENTRY, Σ debits = Σ credits. source_event_id is unique → the same PSP event can never be posted twice.
