3.5 Consistency model

Data Consistency needed Mechanism
Slot uniqueness Strong Exclusion constraint (single primary) + Redis hold
Clinical record writes Strong, no lost update Single primary, If-Match optimistic concurrency, read-your-writes routing for the author
Prescription legal status Strong in the Prescription service; propagated to pharmacies in seconds State machine + outbox + reconciliation every 5 min
Payments and ledger Strong, effect exactly once Idempotency keys, unique source event IDs, balanced entries
Booking + payment across services Eventually consistent business transaction Saga with compensation (release slot, void authorisation)
Availability cache, directory, timeline projection Eventual (seconds) Recomputed from events; rebuildable
Critical (emergency) summary Eventual (p99 < 5 s) Event-driven projection; the emergency view also lists changes of the last 24 h read directly from the replica
Notification preferences replica Eventual (seconds) PreferencesUpdated events

3.6 Identifiers

  • UUIDv7 for every entity: globally unique across services and regions, time-ordered (good index locality), not guessable in sequence — never auto-increment integers exposed in URLs (prevents enumeration attacks).
  • Patient identity: MedX patient ID (internal, pseudonymous) + national health identifier (INS) stored encrypted and used only for identity matching and national-service exchanges.
  • Human-facing references (invoice numbers, prescription verification codes) are separate, purpose-specific identifiers.

3.7 Data lifecycle and retention

Data Retention End of life Basis
Medical record (resources, documents, transcripts, prescriptions) 20 years after the last encounter (France; longer for minors), configurable per jurisdiction; legal hold possible Crypto-shredding (patient keys destroyed) then physical deletion Public-health law
Chat hot store 30 days (transcript already archived in the record) TTL expiry Minimisation
Video/audio Not recorded — Privacy by design
Appointments 5 years after the appointment, then anonymised for statistics Anonymisation job Evidence of care, disputes
User account (patient) While active; closed after 3 years of inactivity with prior notice Deletion of C2 data; medical record kept under its own rule GDPR storage limitation
Practitioner identity As long as records reference the practitioner Kept (attribution of records) Integrity of records
Invoices, ledger 10 years Deletion Commercial law
Payment tokens Until removed by the user, or 13 months after last use Deleted at the PSP and locally PCI DSS, minimisation
Notification log 13 months TTL expiry Evidence of delivery
Audit trail ≥ 6 years, configurable up to record retention Object Lock expiry then deletion Accountability
Technical/security logs 12 months Deletion Security investigations
Backups PITR 35 days · daily snapshots 35 days · monthly snapshots 12 months Automatic expiry (immutable until then) Recovery
Key registries (wrapped patient keys) Backups kept 35 days only Expiry Makes crypto-shredding effective in backups
De-identified analytics Anonymous data: unlimited · pseudonymised datasets: 2 years Deletion Research, statistics

Right to erasure vs medical retention — GDPR art. 17(3) exempts data that must be kept for healthcare or legal obligations: a patient can close their account and delete contact data, but the medical record stays under its legal retention (the patient is told so clearly).

3.8 Data integrity mechanisms

Threat Mechanisms
Concurrent edits (lost update) Optimistic concurrency (If-Match/version), single primary for writes
Invalid or inconsistent data FHIR profile & terminology validation, foreign keys and check constraints, state machines, exclusion constraint
Partial failures between services Transactional outbox, idempotent consumers, sagas with compensation, reconciliation jobs
Silent tampering (insider, compromised admin) Append-only history, per-patient hash chains, daily Merkle root signed in HSM and timestamped, WORM audit archive, verification jobs
Corrupted files SHA-256 checksum at upload, at every download and in weekly scrub jobs; object versioning
Accidental or malicious deletion, ransomware No delete privilege for application roles on history; Object Lock (compliance mode); immutable, cross-account backup vault; deletion protection on databases
Loss of a zone or region Synchronous standby in another AZ (RPO 0), cross-region replicas (RPO ≤ 1 min), replicated object storage
Undetected backup failure Automated restore tests every week (sample) and full restore drill every quarter, with integrity verification

3.9 Backup and recovery

Store Backup Restore objective
PostgreSQL (all services) Continuous WAL archiving → PITR 35 days; daily snapshots; monthly snapshots 12 months; copies in the immutable vault (other account, other region) Point-in-time restore of one service without touching others
Cassandra Daily snapshots + incremental backups to object storage Chat is rebuildable from record transcripts; notification log is non-critical
Object storage Versioning + Object Lock + cross-region replication + vault copy Object or version restore; region failover
Kafka Not backed up as a store (events are also in databases); MirrorMaker to DR for continuity Replay from outboxes if needed
Redis / OpenSearch Not backed up (derived data) — rebuilt from systems of record Rebuild jobs (minutes to hours)
Keys (KMS/HSM) Provider-managed, multi-region keys; Vault DR replication —

3.10 Data residency and replication

  • All health data is stored and processed in the EEA, in HDS-certified regions (primary France, DR Germany).
  • Cross-region replication is encrypted in transit and re-encrypted at rest with multi-region keys.
  • Expansion to another jurisdiction (e.g., the US) is done with a separate regional cell: a full copy of the platform with its own data, keys and compliance scope (HIPAA); only non-personal configuration is shared globally. Patient data never flows between cells except at the patient's request.

4. Scalability & Performance

Deliverable 4. How MedX handles a growing user base and keeps its performance — with numbers. Targets come from §0.7 capacity targets and §0.8 service levels.

4.1 Strategy in one page

Lever What MedX does
Scale out, not up Stateless services on Kubernetes, autoscaled on the metric that really limits each one (requests, connections, queue lag, participants).
Separate what scales differently Media plane, records, notifications and payments have independent scaling and failure domains.
Keep the hot path short Local token validation and policy decisions, pre-computed availability and emergency summaries, at most two synchronous hops.
Absorb peaks asynchronously Kafka and priority lanes turn spikes into backlogs that drain in seconds, never into errors.
Protect what matters most Bulkheads and load-shedding order: emergency access → ongoing consultations → clinical writes → booking → the rest.
Grow in steps with explicit triggers Replicas → partitioning → sharding by patient → regional cells; each step triggered by measured thresholds.
Prove it continuously Load, soak, chaos and WebRTC tests at 2× the forecast peak before each major release; SLOs with error budgets.

4.2 Workload model

Pattern Description Design response
Daily cycle Peaks Monday 8–10 am and 6–8 pm; nights ≈ 5 % of peak Scheduled pre-scaling + autoscaling; batch jobs at night
Seasonal surges Flu season, epidemics: ×3 to ×5 demand in days Surge playbook (§4.10), headroom ×2 by design, DR region can absorb read traffic
Reminder bursts Thousands of reminders due at round hours Jittered sending window, dedicated notification lane
Read-heavy clinical data Records read ≈ 5–10× more than written Replicas, projections, patient-scoped queries
Long-lived connections WebSocket for chat/status, WebRTC for media Dedicated gateways and media nodes scaled on connections/participants

4.4 Performance objectives and latency budgets

SLOs are defined per criticality tier in §0.8. Each critical request has a latency budget that the design must respect:

Emergency critical summary (target p95 < 300 ms server-side)

Step Budget
Gateway: JWT signature (cached JWKS), DPoP check, rate limit ≤ 5 ms
mTLS hop to the Emergency Access pod ≤ 2 ms
OPA decision (sidecar, in memory) ≤ 1 ms
Insert grant + audit outbox (synchronous Multi-AZ commit) ≤ 15 ms
Read pre-computed summary (one indexed row, local replica) ≤ 10 ms
Unwrap patient key (in-memory cache; KMS on a miss) ≤ 1 ms (≤ 30 ms on miss)
Decrypt, apply obligations, serialise ≤ 5 ms
Typical total ≈ 40–70 ms, leaving a wide margin under 300 ms

Booking confirmation (target p95 < 800 ms excluding 3-D Secure) — hold ≤ 20 ms (Redis + insert), payment authorisation 300–600 ms (PSP, the dominant term), commit + outbox ≤ 20 ms.

Chat message (target p95 < 500 ms) — gateway ≤ 5 ms, authorisation + encryption ≤ 3 ms, Cassandra write (LOCAL_QUORUM) ≤ 10 ms, pub/sub fan-out ≤ 5 ms; the rest is network.

4.5 Scaling by layer and by service

Layer Mechanism
Edge CDN offloads static assets; managed WAF/load balancers scale automatically; gateway pods autoscaled on RPS and CPU.
Services Kubernetes Horizontal Pod Autoscaler on CPU and custom metrics (RPS, p95 latency, Kafka lag via KEDA); cluster autoscaler adds nodes; pod anti-affinity spreads replicas across 3 AZs; minimum 3 replicas for Tier 0/1.
Data Vertical sizing + read replicas + connection pooling (PgBouncer) + partitioning; sharding path for Records (§4.7).
Events Topics partitioned by aggregate key (12–48 partitions); consumer groups scale up to the partition count.
Real-time WebSocket pods scaled on open connections; Redis pub/sub cluster for fan-out.
Media SFU nodes scaled on participants and egress bandwidth; region-aware placement; drain before scale-in.
Service Load driver Autoscaling signal Replicas (Year 3, min–max) Main bottleneck → mitigation
API Gateway Requests RPS, CPU 6 – 40 —
Real-time Gateway Connections Connections per pod (~25 k) 4 – 20 Memory per connection → lean frames, heartbeats
① User Management + IdP Logins, refreshes CPU 3 – 12 Password hashing CPU → rate limits, passkeys
② Scheduling Searches, bookings RPS 3 – 30 Availability computation → pre-computed Redis cache
③ Consultation (control plane) Joins, chat RPS, WebSocket messages 3 – 20 —
Media plane (SFU + TURN) Participants Participants per node, bandwidth 10 – 200 nodes Bandwidth → simulcast, adaptive stream, audio-only
④ Patient Records Reads RPS, p95 latency 4 – 30 Database → replicas, projections, sharding path
Emergency Access Break-glass requests Reserved capacity + RPS 3 per region (fixed floor) – 12 Isolated by design (bulkhead)
⑤ Prescription Writes, checks RPS 3 – 12 Drug checks → cached reference data
⑥ Pharmacy Interface Webhooks, status updates Queue lag 2 – 12 Slow pharmacy systems → asynchronous webhooks
⑦ Notification Events Consumer lag per priority lane 2 – 40 Provider rate limits → two providers per channel
⑧ Billing & Payment Payments RPS 3 – 8 PSP latency → asynchronous capture
Audit Trail Audit events Consumer lag 2 – 10 Object-storage writes → 1-minute batches

4.6 Caching strategy

Cache Content Location Freshness Health data?
CDN App bundles, images Edge Versioned, immutable No
Keys & policies JWKS, OPA bundles In-process 5 min / pulled every 60 s No
Availability Free slots per doctor and day (60 days) Redis Recomputed on events (seconds) No patient data
Directory Doctor public profiles + next free slot OpenSearch Event-driven No (public)
Drug reference Drug catalogue, interactions In-process + OpenSearch Daily refresh No
Emergency summary International Patient Summary per patient PostgreSQL projection + replicas Event-driven (p99 < 5 s) Yes — encrypted
Data keys Unwrapped patient/file keys Service memory only ≤ 5 min, bounded LRU Key material, never persisted
Inventory Availability level per pharmacy and item Redis 15 min No

Rules — no health data in shared caches (the encrypted emergency summary is the only exception); responses with personal data carry Cache-Control: no-store; caches use jittered TTLs and request coalescing to avoid stampedes; every cache is rebuildable from its system of record.

4.7 Database scaling path

Stage Trigger (measured) Action
1 — Launch — One Multi-AZ primary (synchronous standby) per service; Records with 2 read replicas; PgBouncer; statement_timeout and connection quotas per service
2 — Growth Records > 2 TB, replica lag > 1 s, or primary CPU > 60 % at peak Larger instances, more replicas, partition pruning, older history partitions moved to a cheaper storage tier
3 — Scale-out Records writes > ~5 k/s or > 20 TB Shard by patient_id hash (e.g., Citus or application-level routing); each shard with its own replicas — nearly every query is patient-scoped, so shards are independent
4 — New jurisdiction New country or regulation New regional cell (§4.12)

Query hygiene is part of the definition of done: indexes reviewed with EXPLAIN in CI for new queries, pg_stat_statements dashboards, keyset pagination (no deep OFFSET), no N+1 access patterns.

4.8 Video at scale

  • One room per SFU node for 1-to-1 consultations (no cross-node forwarding); multi-party rooms (interpreter) can cascade across nodes.
  • Placement chooses the region with the lowest measured RTT for both participants, then the least-loaded node (CPU, bandwidth, participants).
  • Simulcast + dynacast + adaptive stream send each receiver only the resolution its screen and network need; average received bitrate ~1.2 Mbit/s instead of 2.5 Mbit/s for full 720p.
  • Audio-first: under congestion video degrades first; below ~150 kbit/s the call becomes audio-only.
  • TURN fleet sized for ~20 % of sessions relayed; TURN over TLS 443 for restrictive networks.
  • Scale-in by draining: a node marked for removal accepts no new rooms and is removed when its last call ends.
  • Load testing: headless-browser bots generate thousands of simultaneous calls with injected packet loss and jitter; the node capacity figure (~200 participants per 8 vCPU) is re-measured at every SFU upgrade.
  • Cost lever to evaluate: direct peer-to-peer media for 1-to-1 calls when networks allow would cut SFU egress, at the price of weaker quality monitoring and control — kept as an optimisation, not the baseline.

4.9 High availability and disaster recovery

Component Within the region (AZ failure) Across regions (region failure)
Gateways, services ≥ 3 replicas over 3 AZs; load balancer health checks Pre-deployed in DR, scaled up by the runbook
Emergency Access, IdP ≥ 3 replicas over 3 AZs Active in both regions (DNS health-checked routing)
PostgreSQL Synchronous standby in another AZ, automatic failover < 60 s (RPO 0) Asynchronous cross-region replica (lag < 1 s, RPO ≤ 1 min), promoted by the runbook
Redis Replicas in other AZs, automatic failover Rebuilt (derived data)
Kafka 3 brokers / 3 AZs, RF 3, min.insync.replicas = 2 MirrorMaker 2 to the DR cluster
Cassandra RF 3 across AZs, LOCAL_QUORUM Second datacenter in DR (asynchronous)
Object storage Regional service (multi-AZ by design) Cross-region replication
Media plane Nodes in 3 AZs, clients reconnect Media nodes in DR scale up

Regional failover runbook (rehearsed twice a year):

  1. Detection by synthetic probes and health checks → incident declared, communication started.
  2. Tier 0 continues immediately: emergency access and sign-in are already served by the DR region.
  3. Promote DR database replicas for Tier 1 services (scripted, in dependency order), switch producers to the DR Kafka cluster (translated consumer offsets).
  4. Scale DR Kubernetes node groups to production size (pre-approved capacity reservations) → Tier 1 back ≤ 1 h.
  5. Restore Tier 2 services and rebuild derived stores (caches, search) → Tier 2 back ≤ 4 h.
  6. Fail back after recovery with reverse replication, outside peak hours.

4.10 Resilience patterns and graceful degradation

  • Timeouts everywhere (no call without a deadline), retries with exponential backoff and jitter only for idempotent operations, circuit breakers in the mesh, bulkheads (separate pools and deployments for the emergency path and each priority lane), idempotency keys on every create.
  • Load-shedding order under extreme load, enforced by gateway route priorities, Kubernetes priority classes and queue lanes: ① emergency access → ② ongoing consultations → ③ clinical writes (notes, prescriptions) → ④ booking → ⑤ non-critical notifications → ⑥ analytics and exports.
Failure Degraded behaviour
Payment provider down Holds keep slots; retry; optional "pay later" booking for returning patients
Calendar provider down Last known busy times used; doctor warned that sync is delayed
SMS / e-mail provider down Automatic failover to the second provider; in-app notifications continue
Drug database down Prescribing possible only after explicit acknowledgement that checks are unavailable
Event bus unavailable Core transactions continue; events wait in outboxes; notifications and projections catch up
Records primary database down Automatic failover (< 60 s); reads continue on replicas; emergency access unaffected
Media node failure Clients reconnect to another node within seconds
Search cluster down Fallback search by specialty served from PostgreSQL
Whole region down Tier 0 continues in DR; Tier 1 ≤ 1 h; Tier 2 ≤ 4 h

Surge playbook (epidemic, ×3–×5 demand): scheduled pre-scaling; "surge mode" raising autoscaling floors; additional on-call doctors in the urgent queue; feature flags that switch off non-essential features (exports, recommendations); a virtual waiting room in front of booking if needed, so the platform stays responsive for people already in care.

4.11 Performance engineering practice

Practice Cadence
Performance budgets checked in CI (key endpoints, p95) Every merge
Load tests at 1× and 2× forecast peak (k6 / Gatling), including WebRTC bots with network impairment Every major release
Soak tests (24 h) for leaks and slow degradation Monthly
Chaos experiments (pod kill, AZ loss, latency injection, dependency outage) Monthly in staging, quarterly game days in production
DR failover drill Twice a year
Capacity review vs forecast (users, bandwidth, storage) Monthly
SLO review with error budgets — feature work pauses for reliability when a budget is burnt Weekly

4.12 Growth beyond Year 3 — cells

When MedX outgrows one region or enters a new jurisdiction, it scales by cells: a cell is a complete, isolated copy of the platform (services, data, keys) serving a population (a country, or a shard of patients). A thin global routing layer — holding no health data — sends each user to their home cell. Cells limit the blast radius of any incident, keep data residency simple (a US cell under HIPAA, EU cells under GDPR/HDS) and turn growth into a repeatable deployment rather than a redesign.

4.13 Cost efficiency

  • Autoscaling floors lowered at night; non-production environments scaled to zero outside working hours.
  • Reserved capacity for the steady baseline; spot/preemptible capacity only for stateless, non-critical workloads (never Tier 0, never media).
  • Storage lifecycle: documents older than 1 year move to an infrequent-access tier, older than 5 years to an archive tier — with Object Lock retention preserved.
  • Media bandwidth is the largest variable cost: simulcast, audio-only fallback and tuned bitrates are both quality and cost measures; cost per consultation is tracked as a KPI.

5. Security & Compliance

Deliverable 5. Security protocols, encryption methods and compliance measures that protect MedX's health data. This is where the High-priority requirements H1 (data privacy), H3 (emergency access controls), H4 (authentication & authorization) and H5 (integrity) become concrete controls.

5.1 Objectives and principles

Objective Meaning for MedX
Confidentiality Health data is seen only by the patient and the professionals who treat them, for a legitimate purpose.
Integrity Records, prescriptions and payments are complete, correct and tamper-evident.
Availability Critical information is reachable in an emergency, even during failures (Tier 0).
Accountability Every access to health data can be attributed, explained and reviewed.
Privacy Collect the minimum, use it only for its purpose, keep it only as long as required, respect patients' rights.

Principles: defence in depth · zero trust (no implicit trust from the network: every call is authenticated, authorised and encrypted) · least privilege · deny by default · privacy by design and by default · assume breach (limit blast radius, detect fast, recover from immutable backups) · security as code (policies, infrastructure and controls versioned and tested).

Framework Why it applies Key obligations How the design complies

HDS certification (French Public Health Code, art. L.1111-8) Hosting health data of French patients Hosting by HDS-certified providers; HDS v2 (2024) requires hosting in the EEA; MedX certified for the activities it operates itself HDS-certified cloud regions (France + Germany); only certified services used for PHI; MedX certification plan (§5.12)
National e-health frameworks (ANS: PGSSI-S, INS, Pro Santé Connect, interoperability framework) French health information systems Security policy, national patient identifier, professional authentication, interoperable formats PGSSI-S-aligned policies, INS in the Patient resource, Pro Santé Connect federation, FHIR/IPS model

5.3 Threat model

Built with STRIDE on the architecture's data flows; the table lists the threats with the highest impact on MedX.

# Threat Example Main mitigations Residual risk
T1 Account takeover Credential stuffing on patients, phishing a doctor MFA (phishing-resistant for professionals), breached-password check, rate limiting, DPoP-bound tokens, new-device alerts Low
T2 Broken object-level authorization Changing an ID in a URL to read another patient's record ABAC decision on every object, UUIDs, negative authorization tests in CI, gateway schema validation Low
T3 Insider snooping Staff or doctor browsing a celebrity's record No staff access to PHI, care-grant model, audit of every read, UEBA alerts, patient-visible access log, sanctions Medium → Low
T4 Ransomware / destructive attack Encryption or deletion of databases and backups Immutable cross-account backup vault, Object Lock, least privilege, segmentation, EDR, tested restores Low
T5 Data exfiltration Leaked snapshot, misconfigured bucket, compromised service Per-patient application encryption (stolen data is ciphertext), KMS key policies, egress allow-lists, CSPM, DLP on logs Low
T6 Injection & web attacks SQL injection, XSS, SSRF Parameterised queries, output encoding, strict CSP, WAF, SAST/DAST, egress control Low
T7 Eavesdropping on consultations Man-in-the-middle on video DTLS-SRTP + E2EE, TLS 1.3, certificate pinning in apps Low
T8 Malicious file upload Malware disguised as a medical PDF Quarantine, antivirus, magic-byte type checks, PDF sanitisation, isolated scanners Low
T9 Supply-chain compromise Malicious dependency or base image Dependency scanning, pinned versions, SBOM, signed images verified at admission, build provenance Medium
T10 DDoS and abuse Booking bots, directory scraping CDN/WAF, bot management, rate limits, virtual waiting room Low
T11 Prescription fraud Forged or re-used prescriptions Signed prescriptions, verification endpoint with live status, QR codes without content Low
T12 Break-glass abuse Fake emergency to read a record Entitlement, justification, step-up MFA, real-time alert, patient notice, mandatory review, sanctions Low–Medium
T13 Payment fraud Stolen cards 3-D Secure (SCA), PSP risk scoring, velocity limits Low
T14 Leakage through notifications An SMS revealing a diagnosis to a family member No PHI in external messages, allow-listed template variables Low
T15 Cloud misconfiguration Public bucket, disabled logging Organisation guardrails (deny public access, deny disabling encryption/logging), IaC scanning, CSPM Low

5.4 Identity and access management

Details are in §2.1 User Management; the security-relevant rules are:

  • Authentication assurance — patients: password/passkey + risk-based MFA; professionals: phishing-resistant MFA always (passkeys, security keys, professional smart card via Pro Santé Connect); prescription signing and break-glass require a fresh hardware-bound authentication (step-up within 15 minutes). Short-lived, audience- restricted, DPoP- or certificate-bound tokens.
  • Authorization — RBAC for coarse permissions + ABAC (care relationship, consent, purpose of use, sensitivity labels, organisation) evaluated by OPA next to every service; deny by default; obligations for masking.
  • Privileged access — no standing administrator access to production: just-in-time elevation with approval, MFA, a 4-hour maximum and session recording; platform administrators cannot read PHI (application-level encryption keys are not usable by their roles).
  • Service identities — SPIFFE identities through the mesh (mTLS), mesh authorisation policies define which service may call which; one cloud IAM role per service with least privilege (e.g., only the Records role may use the Records KEK).
  • Lifecycle — automated deprovisioning for staff leavers; monthly registry sync suspends struck-off practitioners; quarterly recertification of entitlements such as emergency_access; segregation of duties between developers, database administrators and key custodians; 4-eyes for sensitive operations.

5.5 Encryption in transit

Channel Protocol Configuration
Apps ↔ edge TLS 1.3 (TLS 1.2 with ECDHE + AEAD suites only for older devices; TLS ≤ 1.1 disabled) HSTS with preload, OCSP stapling, automatic certificate rotation, public-key pinning (with backup keys) in mobile apps
Edge ↔ services, service ↔ service mTLS (service mesh, STRICT mode — plaintext refused) SPIFFE workload identities, certificates rotated every 24 h, authorisation policies per caller
Services ↔ datastores TLS with server verification PostgreSQL sslmode=verify-full; TLS for Redis, Kafka (plus mTLS client authentication), Cassandra (client and inter-node), OpenSearch
Audio/video DTLS-SRTP (mandatory in WebRTC) + E2EE (SFrame) for 1-to-1 when supported TURN over TLS 443 on restrictive networks
Pharmacy systems, partners mTLS + OAuth 2.0 with certificate-bound tokens Outbound webhooks signed HMAC-SHA256 with timestamp and replay protection
External providers (SMS, e-mail, push, calendars, PSP) TLS 1.2+ with certificate validation No PHI in payloads; SMTP with MTA-STS, SPF/DKIM/DMARC
Region ↔ region replication TLS Re-encrypted at rest with multi-region keys

Cipher policy — TLS 1.3 suites (AES-128/256-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305) with forward secrecy (X25519, P-256). Because health data must stay confidential for decades, MedX enables hybrid post-quantum key exchange (X25519 + ML-KEM) wherever clients and load balancers support it, against "harvest now, decrypt later" attacks (crypto-agility is a design requirement: algorithms are configuration, not code).

5.6 Encryption at rest and key management

Two independent layers

Layer Scope Mechanism Protects against
1 — Storage encryption Every volume, database, snapshot, backup, object, Kafka log, Redis, Cassandra, OpenSearch AES-256 with customer-managed KMS keys Lost disks, stolen snapshots, provider-side media access
2 — Application (envelope) encryption C4 data: sensitive FHIR elements, documents, chat, national identifiers, contact data AES-256-GCM in the service with per-patient / per-file / per-consultation data keys; additional authenticated data binds ciphertext to its record Database-level compromise, over-privileged administrators, misconfigured replicas or exports, SQL injection returning raw rows

Key hierarchy — root keys in HSMs (FIPS 140-3 level 3) → KEKs in KMS per service × environment × data class (never exported) → data keys (DEKs) generated by KMS, stored only in wrapped form next to the data → ciphertext.

Lifecycle step Rule
Generation In the HSM/KMS only; no application-generated long-term keys
Access KMS key policies: only the owning service's role may decrypt with its KEK; key administrators cannot use keys to decrypt; every use logged in the security account
Caching Unwrapped DEKs kept in process memory ≤ 5 minutes (bounded LRU), never written to disk or logs
Rotation KEKs rotated automatically every year (old versions kept for decryption; DEKs re-wrapped progressively); DEKs rotated on suspicion of compromise
Separation Production keys unusable from non-production accounts → a production snapshot cannot be decrypted outside production
Disaster recovery Multi-region keys for the DR region; Vault replicated
Destruction Crypto-shredding: at the end of retention the patient's data keys are destroyed; key registries keep only 35 days of backups, so every remaining copy of the data — replicas, backups — becomes unreadable

Other protections — passwords hashed with Argon2id; secrets in Vault (dynamic database credentials, Transit encryption for integration tokens); payment cards tokenised by the PSP; mobile apps keep no health data beyond the session except documents the user explicitly downloads, protected by OS keystore-backed file encryption and wiped on logout.

5.7 Data masking, redaction and anonymization

Dynamic masking (M4) — the policy engine returns masking obligations applied before any response leaves a service (support agents see +33 6 •• •• •• 42, pharmacists see no diagnosis, break-glass excludes psychotherapy notes…). The complete matrix is in §2.4.

Redaction — documents shared or exported can have tagged sections removed; PDF redaction removes the text layer (true redaction, not a black rectangle); logs and traces never contain PHI (allow-listed fields, tokenised identifiers, automated scanner on log samples).

Anonymization for staging and demo (L4) — rule: production health data never leaves production.

Environment Data Controls
Development, staging, demo Synthetic patients (e.g., Synthea FHIR bundles) and generated appointments, prescriptions, payments; demo tenant watermarked "DEMO" Separate accounts, no network path or key access to production
Performance tests needing realistic distributions Anonymised extracts produced by the pipeline above k ≥ 10 on quasi-identifiers, l-diversity on sensitive attributes, documented re-identification risk assessment, DPO approval, dataset expiry
Analytics and research Anonymised data; pseudonymised data only inside production-grade controls and with legal basis/consent Purpose registry, access reviews

5.8 Application and API security

  • Secure development lifecycle — threat modelling for each significant feature, security champions in every team, OWASP ASVS level 2 baseline and level 3 for User Management, Records, Emergency Access and Prescription; security acceptance criteria in the definition of done.
  • Automated checks in CI — SAST, dependency scanning (SCA), secret scanning, infrastructure-as-code scanning, container image scanning; DAST and API fuzzing against staging; authorization test suites with negative cases (patient A must never read patient B).
  • Independent testing — penetration test before launch and every year, after major changes; bug-bounty programme after launch.
  • API protections (OWASP API Top 10) — object- and property-level authorization, response allow-lists (no mass exposure), explicit request models (no mass assignment), rate limits and quotas, SSRF protection through an egress gateway with allow-listed destinations, complete API inventory in the gateway.
  • Web — strict nonce-based CSP, Trusted Types, SRI, HSTS, frame-ancestors 'none' (except the PSP component), SameSite cookies, CSRF tokens for cookie sessions.
  • Mobile (OWASP MASVS) — certificate pinning, app attestation, sensitive screens hidden from screenshots and task switcher, no health data in device logs, rooted/jailbroken devices treated as a risk signal.
  • Supply chain — pinned dependencies, SBOM for every image, minimal (distroless) base images patched weekly, signed images verified at admission, build provenance (SLSA), reviewed changes only (protected branches).

5.9 Infrastructure and network security

  • Landing zone — separate accounts (production, DR, security & log archive, shared services, non-production) under organisation guardrails: deny public storage, deny disabling encryption or logging, deny regions outside the EEA.
  • Network — private subnets for all services and datastores; public exposure limited to load balancers and media nodes; Kubernetes network policies default deny; mesh authorisation policies; private endpoints to cloud services; egress only through controlled gateways with allow-lists.
  • Workload hardening — CIS benchmarks, Pod Security "restricted" profile, non-root and read-only containers, seccomp/AppArmor, runtime threat detection, EDR on nodes; vulnerability SLAs: critical < 7 days, high < 30 days.
  • Staff access — identity-aware zero-trust proxy (no VPN, no SSH); production access only through JIT elevation.
  • Physical security — inherited from the HDS / ISO 27001-certified cloud provider.

5.10 Logging, detection and incident response

  • Security logging — authentication events, authorisation denials, admin actions, KMS usage, network flows, audit trail; shipped to the security account (immutable, 12 months for technical logs, ≥ 6 years for the audit trail).
  • Detection (SIEM + UEBA) — break-glass events, access without care relationship attempts, mass record reads or exports, impossible travel, MFA disabled, privilege escalation, anomalous KMS decrypt volumes, new public endpoint.
  • Response — documented plans for data breach, ransomware, account takeover and break-glass abuse; 24/7 on-call; severity levels; forensic readiness (retained logs, snapshot procedures); tabletop exercises twice a year.
Notification duty Deadline
GDPR — supervisory authority (CNIL) 72 h after awareness (art. 33)
GDPR — affected patients Without undue delay when the risk is high (art. 34)
NIS2 — national CSIRT / authority Early warning 24 h, notification 72 h, final report 1 month
French health sector — serious incidents Declaration to the health authorities' incident portal / CERT Santé
HIPAA (US cell) Individuals within 60 days; HHS as required

Requirement Controls How it is verified
H1 Data privacy (encryption at rest & in transit) TLS 1.3 / mTLS everywhere; AES-256 storage encryption; per-patient envelope encryption; HSM-backed keys; no PHI outside the clinical zone Encryption compliance checks on 100 % of stores; TLS configuration scans; mesh in STRICT mode; PHI-in-logs scanner

6. Architecture Decisions & Trade-offs

Why the design looks the way it does. Each decision is traced to MedX's priorities (Appendix 2) and states what was given up — a design without acknowledged costs is not a design.

6.1 The tensions that shaped the architecture

Tension How MedX resolves it Priority that decided
Privacy ⟷ emergency availability Access in an emergency is never blocked by a workflow; it is narrow, time-boxed, fully audited and reviewed (break-glass). H1 + H3
Security ⟷ usability Strict for professionals (phishing-resistant MFA, step-up), smooth for patients (passkeys, risk-based MFA, biometrics). H4, then M1–M2
Consistency ⟷ availability Strong consistency where errors harm (records writes, bookings, prescriptions, payments); eventual elsewhere; the emergency path favours availability with bounded staleness (< 5 s). H2, H3, H5
Isolation ⟷ operational complexity Eight business services (no more), grouped in zones, on a shared golden-path platform. H1, H3
Resilience ⟷ cost Active-active only for Tier 0 (emergency access, sign-in); warm standby for the rest. H3
Rich messages ⟷ confidentiality Generic external messages + deep links into the authenticated app. H1
Build ⟷ buy Build what is differentiating or sensitive (records, emergency access, care workflows, policies); buy commodities (IdP software, PSP, messaging, SFU software). All — frees capacity for High priorities

6.2 Decision log

ADR Decision Priority link Main alternative rejected What we give up
01 Microservices by bounded context, grouped into security zones H1, H3, scalability Modular monolith Simpler operations
02 HL7 FHIR R4 (+ IPS) as the clinical model, on PostgreSQL H2, interoperability Custom relational schema Some storage efficiency
03 PostgreSQL by default; specialised stores only when justified H5, simplicity NoSQL-first polyglot persistence Extreme write scale by default
04 Append-only clinical history + hash chains + signed daily anchors H2, H5 In-place updates + audit table ~30 % more storage
05 Two encryption layers with per-patient envelope keys H1 Storage encryption only Complexity, ~1 ms per request
06 Break-glass with post-hoc review on an isolated, two-region Tier-0 path H3 Pre-approval workflow Some risk of misuse (mitigated)
07 Proven IdP (Keycloak) + OPA policies (RBAC + ABAC) enforced locally H4 Custom auth; RBAC only Running a stateful IdP cluster
08 Event-driven integration (Kafka) with transactional outbox H5, scalability Synchronous call chains Eventual consistency to reason about
09 Self-hosted WebRTC SFU (LiveKit), E2EE by default for 1-to-1 H1, M2 Video CPaaS; P2P; MCU Operating media servers; no recording
10 No PHI outside the trust boundary (messages, calendars, events, logs) H1 Rich notifications Some convenience
11 PSP-hosted payment fields → PCI DSS SAQ A L5, H1 Handling card data Control over payment UI
12 Multi-AZ everywhere + warm-standby DR; active-active only for Tier 0 H3, H5 Full active-active RTO of 1–4 h for Tier 1–2
13 Synthetic data by default outside production; anonymisation under DPO control L4, H1 Masked copies of production Some realism in tests
14 Deliver by priority: secure core → care workflows → ecosystem All Feature-first MVP Later commercial launch

6.3 Decision records

ADR-01 — Microservices by bounded context, grouped into security zones

  • Context — eight business capabilities with very different data sensitivity (PHI, card-adjacent, contact data), load profiles (video bandwidth vs record reads vs payment correctness) and criticality (Tier 0 to 2).
  • Decision — one service per Appendix-1 component, plus platform services; zones (identity, clinical, engagement, payment) with dedicated node pools and network policies.
  • Alternatives — monolith (one blast radius); modular monolith (good start, but no isolation of the emergency path nor of compliance scopes); function-as-a-service (cold starts, poor fit for WebRTC/WebSocket).
  • Consequences — ✅ isolation of PHI and failures, independent scaling and releases; ❌ distributed-systems complexity → golden-path template, service mesh, platform team, strict limit on the number of services.

ADR-02 — HL7 FHIR R4 (+ International Patient Summary) as the clinical data model

  • Context — records must be complete, valid, versioned and exchangeable with national services and hospitals; emergency access needs a standard summary.
  • Decision — FHIR resources stored by a FHIR server (HAPI FHIR on PostgreSQL); IPS profile for the critical summary; national profiles for validation.
  • Alternatives — custom schema (faster to start, costly integrations later); document database (flexible, but weaker transactions and one more technology).
  • Consequences — ✅ interoperability, validation, history and search out of the box; ❌ generic storage is less efficient → UI projections and partitioning.

ADR-03 — PostgreSQL by default, specialised stores only when justified

  • Decision — PostgreSQL for all systems of record; Redis (ephemeral), Cassandra (append-heavy TTL logs), object storage (files), OpenSearch (search) only where PostgreSQL is a poor fit.
  • Why — fewer technologies to secure, certify, back up and staff; constraints and transactions protect integrity (e.g., exclusion constraint against double booking).
  • Consequences — ✅ integrity and simplicity; ❌ extreme write scale needs the sharding path (§4.7).

ADR-04 — Append-only clinical history, hash chains and signed anchors

  • Decision — no in-place update or physical deletion of clinical data during retention; each version chained by hash; daily Merkle root signed in the HSM, timestamped and stored in WORM.
  • Why — H5 data integrity and H2 compliance: history must be provable, not just "logged".
  • Consequences — ✅ tamper evidence even against administrators; ❌ ~30 % extra storage, verification jobs.

ADR-05 — Two encryption layers with per-patient envelope keys

  • Decision — storage encryption everywhere + application-level AES-256-GCM for C4 data with per-patient / per-file / per-consultation keys wrapped by HSM-backed KEKs.
  • Alternatives — storage encryption only (does not protect against database-level compromise or leaked exports); one KMS key per patient (millions of KMS keys: cost and quota limits).
  • Consequences — ✅ stolen data is useless, blast radius of one key = one patient, crypto-shredding at end of retention; ❌ key-management complexity, ~1 ms overhead with key caching, careful key backup policies.

ADR-06 — Break-glass with post-hoc review, on an isolated Tier-0 path

  • Context — H3 requires immediate access for authorised professionals; H1 requires strict confidentiality.
  • Decision — self-service break-glass (entitlement + justification + step-up MFA) → 4-hour read-only grant → pre-computed IPS summary; real-time alert, patient notice, mandatory review within 72 h; separate deployment and database, active in two regions.
  • Alternatives — supervisor pre-approval (too slow at 3 am in an emergency room); open access for all doctors (unacceptable privacy risk).
  • Consequences — ✅ access in seconds, even during failures; ❌ misuse is possible but visible, attributable and sanctioned; one more deployable unit.

ADR-07 — Proven IdP + policy-as-code authorization

  • Decision — Keycloak for authentication (OIDC, MFA, passkeys, federation); OPA sidecars evaluating RBAC + ABAC policies from signed bundles; short-lived tokens validated locally.
  • Alternatives — custom authentication (high risk); RBAC only (cannot express care relationships, consent or emergencies); central authorization server called on every request (latency and single point of failure).
  • Consequences — ✅ strong, standard, testable, fast; ❌ revocation is not instantaneous (bounded by 5–10 min tokens + denylist), a stateful IdP to operate in two regions.

ADR-08 — Event-driven integration with the transactional outbox

  • Decision — services publish domain events (ids and statuses only) through an outbox relayed to Kafka; consumers are idempotent; synchronous calls only when a user is waiting (≤ 2 hops).
  • Alternatives — synchronous chains (cascading failures, tight coupling); publish-after-commit without outbox (lost or phantom events).
  • Consequences — ✅ decoupling, resilience, natural audit feed and projections; ❌ eventual consistency to design for (sagas, reconciliation jobs).

ADR-09 — Self-hosted WebRTC SFU with end-to-end encryption

  • Decision — LiveKit SFU and TURN servers on HDS-certified infrastructure; simulcast and adaptive bitrate; E2EE on by default for 1-to-1 consultations; no recording.
  • Alternatives — CPaaS (fast to integrate, but media processed outside MedX's certified scope and costly at scale — kept as fallback); peer-to-peer mesh (no quality control, relaying issues); MCU (CPU-heavy, breaks E2EE).
  • Consequences — ✅ data sovereignty, confidentiality, cost control; ❌ media operations skills, no server-side recording or transcription while E2EE is on.

ADR-10 — No health data outside the trust boundary

  • Decision — SMS, e-mails, push banners, external calendars, event payloads, logs and traces never contain health data; details are shown only after authentication in the app.
  • Consequences — ✅ removes whole classes of leaks and keeps third-party providers out of the HDS scope; ❌ less informative messages (mitigated by deep links).

ADR-11 — PSP-hosted payment fields (PCI DSS SAQ A)

  • Decision — card data goes from the device to the PSP; MedX stores tokens only; 3-D Secure; own double-entry ledger for money movements.
  • Consequences — ✅ minimal PCI scope and no card data to steal; ❌ payment UI constrained by the PSP components.

ADR-12 — Multi-AZ everywhere, warm-standby DR, active-active only for Tier 0

  • Decision — every tier redundant across 3 AZs (RPO 0 in-region); a second EU region as warm standby (RPO ≤ 1 min); emergency access and sign-in active in both regions.
  • Alternatives — full active-active (multi-master conflicts on clinical data, double cost); single region (unacceptable for Tier 0).
  • Consequences — ✅ emergency access survives a regional outage, costs stay reasonable; ❌ Tier 1 and 2 recover in 1 h and 4 h respectively.

ADR-13 — Synthetic data by default outside production

  • Decision — development, staging and demo use synthetic FHIR patients; realistic datasets only through the anonymisation pipeline, with DPO approval; production keys unusable outside production.
  • Consequences — ✅ no real PHI in non-production, ever; ❌ some edge cases found later → targeted anonymised datasets and production-like load tests.

ADR-14 — Deliver by priority, buy what is not differentiating

  • Decision — secure core first (High), care workflows second (Medium), ecosystem last (Low) — see roadmap. Low-priority capabilities rely on partners (PSP, messaging providers) and enter earlier only as thin slices required by Medium features.
  • Consequences — ✅ the foundations every later feature depends on are right from day one; ❌ commercial launch waits for the secure core (a pilot with partner clinics runs during Phase 2).

8. Roadmap & Risks

How the design is delivered in the order of MedX's priorities, and what could go wrong.

8.1 Delivery principles

  1. High-priority capabilities are foundations, not features: encryption, identity, records, integrity and emergency access are built first and are release gates for everything else.
  2. Medium-priority care workflows are built on top of that foundation.
  3. Low-priority capabilities come last and rely on partners (payment provider, messaging providers). Thin, bought slices enter earlier only when a Medium feature needs them (e.g., a transactional e-mail for a booking confirmation).
  4. Each phase ends with exit criteria that are measured, not declared.

8.2 Phased plan (indicative, kick-off January 2027)

Phase Scope Priorities Exit criteria
0 — Foundations (≈ 2 months) Accounts and guardrails, Kubernetes + mesh (mTLS STRICT), CI/CD with signing and scanning, KMS/HSM + Vault, event bus + outbox relay, audit trail (WORM), Document Store, observability, synthetic data generator H1, H5 (enablers) Every environment built from code; 100 % of stores encrypted; audit events immutable end-to-end
1 — Secure clinical core (≈ 4 months) User Management + Keycloak + OPA; Patient Records (FHIR, versioning, hash chains, per-patient keys, consent, care grants); Emergency Access active in two regions; DR region; DPIA H1–H5 Authorization test suite green; hash-chain verification green; break-glass p95 < 300 ms in both regions; DR drill passed; external pentest with no critical/high finding open
2 — Care workflows (≈ 4 months) Scheduling (holds, saga, waitlist, urgent queue) + calendar connectors; Consultation (SFU, TURN, chat, file sharing, E2EE); Prescription (signing, checks, revoke); masking & redaction; thin transactional notifications M1–M5 Load test at 2× Year-1 peak passed; video quality KPIs met on impaired networks; revocation reaches pharmacy portal < 5 s; pilot with partner clinics
3 — Ecosystem & business (≈ 4 months) Pharmacy portal + partner API + inventory adapters; preferences UI; notification tracking; billing, invoices, refunds, ledger; anonymisation pipeline L1–L6 PCI SAQ A attestation; reconciliation to the cent over 30 days; first PMS vendor integrated; public launch
4 — Scale & expand (continuous) National services (e-prescription, INS, shared record), ISO 27001, sharding when triggered, regional cells, HIPAA-ready US cell — Triggered by growth and market decisions

Team topology — one platform team (infrastructure, security building blocks, observability) and five stream-aligned teams (identity & access · clinical records & emergency · scheduling & consultation · prescription & pharmacy · engagement & billing), plus shared web/mobile front-end capacity; a security champion in each team.

8.4 Open questions for MedX

  1. Legal roles between MedX and practitioners (controller / processor) and resulting HDS certification scope.
  2. Timeline and mandatory scope of national integrations (e-prescription, national identifier, shared record).
  3. Pricing and reimbursement model (patient pays, insurers, third-party payment) — impacts Billing.
  4. Target markets after France and the order of regional cells.
  5. Appetite for AI-assisted features (triage, note-taking): would bring EU AI Act and MDR obligations and constrain end-to-end encryption choices.
